chunks.text: Explore sermon notes from The Kingdom Is Already Yours. Dive deeper with discussion questions and biblical insights.

chunks.title: The Kingdom Is Already Yours | Sermon Notes | The Landmark Church
chunks.text: June 3, 2026The Kingdom Is Already Yours• The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers—it is to him you shall listenThe LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers—it is to him you shall listen — Deuteronomy 18:15• The Beatitudes are the attitudes of the true disciple of Christ.• The kingdom is the root, the conduct is the fruit, and the blessing is the declaration.• To be blessed is to stand under God's favor and approval.Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers; — Psalm 1:1but his delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he meditates day and night. — Psalm 1:2He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither. In all that he does, he prospers. — Psalm 1:3• Knowing what you are only sharpens your knowledge of who God is.Discussion Questions1. The sermon describes the Beatitudes not as a checklist to perform but as a description of someone the kingdom has already laid hold of — the kingdom is the root, the conduct is the fruit, and the blessing is the declaration. How does this change the way you've thought about what it means to live as a follower of Jesus?‍2. Jesus is presented as the greater Moses — the long-awaited prophet of Deuteronomy 18:15 who teaches with divine authority. What does it mean for you personally that the one who speaks in the Sermon on the Mount is not just a moral teacher but the fulfillment of over a thousand years of expectation?‍3. To be "poor in spirit" is described as a conscious awareness of your spiritual bankruptcy before God — not self-loathing, but an honest reckoning with your dependence on Him. Where in your life do you find it hardest to acknowledge that dependence, and what gets in the way?‍4. The sermon connects mourning to the moment a renewed heart sees God's holiness clearly and, in that light, sees its own condition honestly. Have you ever experienced that kind of grief over your own sin? What did it produce in you?‍5. The promise attached to mourning is comfort — and the sermon points to the love of God poured out through His Son as the ground of that comfort. How does knowing that your mourning leads somewhere — that God's comfort is "perfect and without end" — affect the way you sit with grief or conviction right now?

chunks.title: Adam & Rachel Hadley | Missions | Landmark Church
chunks.text: DomesticAdam & Rachel HadleyMissionary Aviation Repair Center's (MARC)|Soldotna, AKLearn MoreLearn MoreLearn MoreAboutGrowing up, Adam attended a flying camp hosted by Moody Bible Institute, where he fell in love with aviation. For years, he dreamed of becoming a missionary pilot.While studying entrepreneurship at Grove City College, Adam discovered a passion for business—and met his future wife, Rachel, a psychology and music major. After graduating in 2013 and getting married in 2014, Adam and Rachel started their company, Home and Healthy, which “enables seniors to live confidently in their home.”The business expanded over time to include home maintenance, lawn care, property management, and, for a season, a nursing agency. During these years, Adam and Rachel also grew in their faith and began hosting and leading a weekly young marrieds Bible study.While on vacation in Anchorage, Alaska, the Lord began to redirect the trajectory of their lives. As Adam was driving around town, he came across the office of Missionary Aviation Repair Center (MARC). After months of communication with MARC, Adam recognized how his nine years of experience in business, accounting, marketing, construction, and home maintenance had uniquely prepared him to serve their mission.Adam stepped into a newly created business manager position at MARC, overseeing marketing, administration, finance, and donor relations. He has worked to strengthen MARC’s operational foundation and financial stability, enabling the organization to continue growing and ministering to communities and villages. Over the past year, Adam has also helped lead financial, legal, and operational updates, along with several facility projects.No items found.SupportSupport Adam & Rachel HadleyHelp support the mission by giving financially to our Missions Fund.Give to MissionsGive to MissionsGive to Missions

chunks.text: InternationalAnthony & Emily HuertaYouth With A Mission (YWAM)|Mazatlán, MexicoLearn MoreLearn MoreLearn MoreAboutAnthony and Emily Huerta are Global Partners serving with Youth With A Mission (YWAM) in Mazatlán, Mexico. Together, they carry a shared calling to mobilize individuals into their God-given destiny—to know God deeply and to make Him known boldly.Emily Huerta is a second-generation missionary whose life has long been marked by obedience and compassion. At just 15 years old, she pioneered KEEPS Ministries in 2008, a work that faithfully served teenage girls in foster care for 17 years across East Texas. Through mentoring, discipleship, and intentional community, KEEPS helped draw God’s daughters out of brokenness and into healing relationship with Him. Alongside this ministry, Emily has led multiple YWAM training schools and has played a vital role in strengthening operations across YWAM campuses, equipping others to thrive in mission.Anthony Huerta encountered Jesus personally on June 16, 2015, while in a year-long Christian rehabilitation program founded by YWAM missionaries. It was there that he experienced the Father’s unconditional love for the first time—an encounter that radically transformed the trajectory of his life. Compelled to live in alignment with this new reality, Anthony joined YWAM in 2016. Since then, he has led mobilization teams around the world, helping people put feet to what God is speaking. His heart burns to see individuals mobilized into missions through evangelism, worship, and training.Anthony and Emily met in 2017 and were married in 2020. In December 2025, they and their two children joyfully joined YWAM Mazatlán, Mexico, stepping into the next chapter of their calling. As a family, they are committed to discipling others and partnering with God in His global mission—to see lives transformed as people everywhere come to know Him and make Him known.‍No items found.SupportSupport Anthony & Emily HuertaHelp support the mission by giving financially to our Missions Fund.Give to MissionsGive to MissionsGive to Missions

chunks.title: Caitlin Terry | Missions | Landmark Church
chunks.text: InternationalCaitlin TerryHydromissions International|New Jersey–Based, Serving InternationallyBlogBlogBlogAboutCaitlin Terry is a licensed Professional Civil Engineer from Vineland, New Jersey, and serves as the Chief Operating Officer of Hydromissions International, a faith-based nonprofit dedicated to bringing water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) solutions to some of the most remote and underserved communities in the world. Although she lives in New Jersey, she regularly travels internationally—typically every month or two—to train teams and oversee projects. In 2026, she will be serving in Uganda, Kenya, Panama, Guatemala, and Nepal, with the possibility of additional work in Mexico and Liberia. Each year varies, but she generally works in five to seven countries annually.For more than 16 years, Caitlin has partnered with local communities to design and implement safe water and sanitation programs using low-tech, highly portable well-drilling methods. By cultivating strong local teams, she helps drill wells, construct sanitation facilities, and teach foundational hygiene principles, always emphasizing long-term sustainability and local ownership.Caitlin has served in villages across five continents. She sees clean water as more than an engineering challenge—it is an opportunity to serve others in the name of Jesus Christ. She is committed to equipping local believers to meet the physical needs of their neighbors while building meaningful relationships that point to the gospel. In many communities, practical acts of service open the door to share the Living Water that only Christ provides.She treasures 1 Peter 4:8–11, which calls believers to love deeply, practice hospitality, and faithfully use the gifts God has given them to serve others, so that “in all things God may be praised through Jesus Christ.”‍No items found.SupportSupport Caitlin TerryHelp support the mission by giving financially to our Missions Fund.Give to MissionsGive to MissionsGive to Missions

chunks.title: “Marks of a Transformed Christian” | Sermon Notes | The Landmark Church
chunks.text: Explore sermon notes from “Marks of a Transformed Christian”. Dive deeper with discussion questions and biblical insights.

chunks.title: “Marks of a Transformed Christian” | Sermon Notes | The Landmark Church
chunks.text: July 22, 2026Topical“Marks of a Transformed Christian”Aaron Capito• The Gospel doesn't just change where we're going - it changes how we're living.Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good. Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor. Do not be slothful in zeal, be fervent in spirit, serve the Lord. Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer. Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality. — Romans 12:9-13• Don't let love be an obligation, but let it be an opportunity.• The greatest evidence that Jesus has transformed our hearts is not merely that we know the gospel, but that we begin to look like the One who gave us the gospel.Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them. Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Live in harmony with one another. Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight. — Romans 12:14-16• Our love for others isn't based on what someone deserves. It's based on the grace we've already received.• Humility is the soil where genuine love grows within us.Repay no evil for evil, but give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all. — Romans 12:17-18Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord." To the contrary, "if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head." Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. — Romans 12:19-21• Christians don't mirror the world—they magnify Christ.• The greatest testimony of Christ's name is a life transformed by His grace.Discussion Questions‍1. Romans 12:9 calls us to let love be genuine — not an obligation, but an opportunity. What's the difference between loving someone out of duty versus loving them as a reflection of Christ's sacrifice? Can you think of a relationship in your life where that shift might change how you show up?‍‍2. The message points out that blessing those who persecute us is rooted in remembering how God responded to us when we were His enemies. How does keeping the gospel in view change the way you respond to people who hurt or frustrate you?‍‍3. Paul calls the church to "live in harmony" — not sameness, but different people unified by one Savior. What does it look like practically in your life or in this community to pursue that kind of harmony, especially with people who are very different from you?‍‍4. The sermon draws a distinction between seeking peace and being responsible for someone else's response to it. Is there a situation in your life where you've been holding onto the outcome instead of simply owning your obedience? What would it look like to trust God with the rest?‍‍5. The closing challenge asks whether our lives are "legible" — whether people can read the love of Christ in the way we speak, forgive, and serve. Honestly, what do you think people "read" when they observe your life? What's one mark of a transformed life from Romans 12 you want to grow in this week?

chunks.text: InternationalGerber & Michelle PerezMission Impact/Healthy Communities|GuatemalaAboutGerber Perez is Guatemalan, and his wife, Michelle, is originally from California. Together with their four children, they have made Guatemala their home as they serve through Mission Impact, where Gerber leads the Healthy Communities ministry. Their mission is to address both the physical and spiritual needs of the communities they serve through healthcare, education, and discipleship.Healthy Communities Guatemala is dedicated to improving lives in rural Guatemala through healthcare, education, and sustainable development. The ministry meets urgent community needs by operating a medical clinic, leading a diabetes support program, and providing a child nutrition program. They also support local schools by supplying teachers and educational resources, and they are actively involved in early childhood education initiatives. Most recently, they built a preschool in an underserved area, giving young children a safe and strong start in their educational journey.Michelle, who holds a Master’s degree in Special Education from the University of California, Santa Barbara, plays a vital role in shaping and strengthening the ministry’s educational programs. With a strong background in community development, Gerber has helped guide Healthy Communities into becoming a trusted and vital support system for some of Guatemala’s most vulnerable communities.Their work is sustained through partnerships with local churches, universities, and volunteers, fostering a collaborative effort to bring lasting change. Through both challenges and victories, they have seen God’s faithful hand at work in the lives of those they serve and in their own family. They remain deeply grateful for the prayers and ongoing support of Landmark Church as they continue their mission of hope and gospel-centered transformation in Guatemala.‍No items found.SupportSupport Gerber & Michelle PerezHelp support the mission by giving financially to our Missions Fund.Give to MissionsGive to MissionsGive to Missions

chunks.text: DomesticJon & Kelly ButhyFellowship Of Christian Athletes (FCA)|South JerseyAboutJon grew up in Olney, Maryland. He attended Montrose Christian School, where he played varsity baseball. Jon studied business management at Montgomery College while working full-time at CVS Pharmacy, where he met his wife, Kelly. They were married in June of 2000.Jon and Kelly both grew up with a Catholic background but did not have a real relationship with God. After many years of infertility, Kelly became pregnant with their first daughter, Brigid. Three years later, after continued infertility and a miscarriage, Kelly became pregnant with twins, Hunter and Holly.The twins were born 16 weeks early, and after only eight months, Hunter passed away due to flu shot complications. Jon and Kelly were devastated. After losing Hunter, Jon’s relationship with God deepened, and he surrendered his life to Christ shortly thereafter.Jon immediately felt called to share the gift of salvation with everyone he met. He and Kelly began teaching weekly Bible classes, and Jon co-directed the Hoping Team Addiction Ministry at Lighthouse Church for five years.In 2019, a full-time Fellowship of Christian Athletes (FCA) staff position became available, and Jon eagerly stepped into the opportunity to spread the Gospel full-time. God has given Jon the privilege of making Gospel ministry his primary focus.As an FCA staff member, Jon’s key objective is to connect Christ to the community by partnering with local schools and churches. He builds relationships with Christian coaches and athletes to establish ministries in public schools. Through these relationships, he has the opportunity to share the Gospel of Jesus Christ and bring God’s Word and prayer to public schools in Cape May, Atlantic, and Cumberland Counties. The ministry is now active in over 20 public schools and continues to grow.On June 16, 2022, God blessed Jon and Kelly with a baby boy, Shiloh Hunter Buthy. Then, on August 29, 2024, God gave them another precious gift—a baby girl named Hosanna-Joy Margaret. God is not only increasing the ministry but also growing their family.‍No items found.SupportSupport Jon & Kelly ButhyHelp support the mission by giving financially to our Missions Fund.Give to MissionsGive to MissionsGive to Missions

chunks.text: July 19, 2026RevelationWhen The Word Consumes YouMatthew Maher• The Old is the New concealed. The New is the Old revealed. The Old + the New is Christ revered.I saw still another mighty angel coming down from heaven, clothed with a cloud. And a rainbow was on his head, his face was like the sun, and his feet like pillars of fire. — Revelation 10:1‍‍He had a little book open in his hand. And he set his right foot on the sea and his left foot on the land… — Revelation 10:2• In his hand: God's prophetic Word. Beneath his feet: God's sovereign world.And cried with a loud voice, as when a lion roars. When he cried out, seven thunders uttered their voices. Now when the seven thunders uttered their voices, I was about to write; but I heard a voice from heaven saying to me, "Seal up the things which the seven thunders uttered, and do not write them." — Revelation 10:3-4• God has revealed everything we need to know, but that doesn't mean we will know everything.The angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised up his hand to heaven and swore by Him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and the things that are in it, the earth and the things that are in it, and the sea and the things that are in it, that there should be delay no longer, but in the days of the sounding of the seventh angel, when he is about to sound, the mystery of God would be finished, as He declared to His servants the prophets. — Revelation 10:5-7• "Just preach the gospel" is the coward's camouflage for: "Don't say anything controversial."Then the voice which I heard from heaven spoke to me again and said, "Go, take the little book which is open in the hand of the angel who stands on the sea and on the earth." So I went to the angel and said to him, "Give me the little book." And he said to me, "Take and eat it; and it will make your stomach bitter, but it will be as sweet as honey in your mouth." — Revelation 10:8-9• The Word of God is not just sweet when you consume it, but also bitter when it consumes you.Then I took the little book out of the angel's hand and ate it, and it was as sweet as honey in my mouth. But when I had eaten it, my stomach became bitter. And he said to me, "You must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, tongues, and kings." — Revelation 10:10-11• The Word of God is a balm and a blade; a hammer and a healer; a fire and a flood.Additional Scriptures Referenced: Revelation 5:1; Ezekiel 2:9 - 3:3; Daniel 7; Revelation 13:1; Revelation 17:15; Revelation 6:10; Hebrews 4:12Discussion Questions1. Where does Revelation 10 fall in the larger flow of Revelation, and what is happening in this interlude between the sixth and seventh trumpets? Why do you think God again "pauses" the sequence of judgments here?‍‍2. Revelation 10 shows that some things were intentionally sealed from John. How does the truth that "God has revealed everything we need to know, but that doesn't mean we will know everything" challenge our need for answers or control?‍‍3. What did you learn about "the mystery of God" and the way God's plan unfolds from Genesis to Revelation? How does seeing the "whole puzzle" broaden your understanding of the gospel?‍‍4. Why is God's Word sometimes sweet to receive but bitter to carry? Where have you personally experienced that tension?‍‍5. What is the difference between tasting the Word and consuming the Word? What are some signs that Scripture has moved beyond information and is actually transforming you?‍‍6. John consumed the Word before he was commissioned to proclaim it. What has God been putting into you through His Word that He may now want to carry through you to someone else?

chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuJuly 15, 2026Topical2026 Camp RecapAaron CapitoAbout the SeriesThis week's focus: now that camp is over, what happens next?Aaron welcomed students back from camp and named the reality that everything they committed to there gets tested the moment they're back in normal life, surrounded by distraction. Rather than repeat last week's camp theme of freedom in Christ, Aaron gave students a challenge: their mission field isn't overseas. It's the people already around them every day.Passages: Romans 10:13-15What Was TaughtGod's plan for your friends is salvationAaron acknowledged that many students made or renewed a decision to follow Christ at camp this year. He connected that to 1 Timothy 2:4, where Paul says God desires all people to be saved and to know the truth, meaning to know Jesus not just as a historical figure but as Savior. Not everyone will accept that gift, but God's desire is still that everyone would. Aaron's point: if that's what God wants, it should be what we want too.God's plan to show your friends salvation is youAaron pointed to Romans 10:13-15, where Paul asks how anyone can call on Jesus if they've never truly heard about Him. Aaron noted that most people have heard the name Jesus, but often only as a historical figure, a curse word, or a myth, not as who He actually is. That means students may be the clearest picture of Jesus the people around them ever get. Aaron used a line from another leader, Matt: you may be the only Bible somebody reads. Every relationship a student has is an opportunity to represent Christ to someone who needs Him.God's plan for your friends begins with your faithfulnessAaron turned to the story of Esther, where Mordecai tells her that if she stays silent, God will still bring deliverance some other way, but she'll have missed the reason she was placed where she was. Aaron's takeaway: God doesn't need us to accomplish His plans. He'll do what He's going to do with or without us. But being invited to take part in that plan is a privilege.Aaron challenged students to carry a sense of urgency about their friends, to let Jesus show up naturally in what they say and do, and to not let fear of rejection hold them back. Being fully known for following Jesus, even if it costs a friendship, matters more than blending in with a crowd that doesn't know Him.Talk About It at HomeThese are the questions the group discussed:Why do you think it's often easier to talk to your friends about sports, movies, or school than it is to talk about Jesus?Think about the people God has already placed in your life, friends, teammates, classmates, or family members. Who do you think needs to hear about Jesus the most, and why do you think God has put you in their life?If you truly believed that God wanted to use you to reach one friend this week, what is one practical step you could take?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:What was your favorite part of camp this year?Who's one friend you talk to almost every day? What do you two usually talk about?Has anyone ever asked you about your faith? What happened?Is there someone you've been meaning to reach out to but haven't yet?‍

chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuAugust 16, 2026Redemption SeriesBalak & BalaamLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight continued the Redemption Series' walk through the wilderness years of Israel, picking up right after the bronze serpent story in Numbers 21, where Israel started trusting God again and began winning battles instead of wandering.Passages: Numbers 22-24, 1 Corinthians 10:1-13What Was TaughtA King Tries to Buy a CurseAs Israel advanced toward Moab, word spread about the battles they had just won. Moab's king, Balak, was terrified he was next. He could not beat Israel with an army, so he hired the closest thing he could find to a weapon: a pagan prophet named Balaam, who claimed he could bless or curse people on behalf of the gods for a price.Balaam Tries to Negotiate With GodWhen Balak's messengers came for Balaam, God told him plainly not to go. Balaam did not say no outright. He sent word back that he would love to help, for the right price, but God would not let him, essentially inviting Balak to raise the offer. Balaam already knew God's answer. He was not seeking God's will. He was hoping to wear God down into a different one.Students heard this compared to asking one parent for permission, getting told no, then quietly asking the other parent an hour later hoping they did not get the memo. That is not seeking permission. It is shopping for a different answer to a question that has already been settled.Eventually God told Balaam to go, but not as approval. It was God giving Balaam over to what he already wanted, letting him walk into what came next.A Donkey Sees What a Prophet CannotOn the road, an angel of the Lord blocked Balaam's path. Balaam's donkey saw the angel three times and tried to avoid it. Balaam could not see it at all and beat the donkey each time. The "spiritual expert" who claimed he could see into the divine realm turned out to be more spiritually blind than his own donkey.Students heard this compared to ignoring a GPS that says "recalculating" because you are positive you know a shortcut. The donkey stopping in the road was God's version of a reroute, a clear signal that something ahead was wrong. Balaam's response was not to ask why. It was to push harder.God gave the donkey the ability to speak, and through that conversation Balaam's eyes were finally opened to the angel standing in the road with a drawn sword, likely a pre-incarnate appearance of Jesus Himself. The angel told Balaam his way was perverse before Him. This was personal: the sin was against God directly. Balaam repented, but even then he hedged, saying he would turn back only if it displeased God. He already knew it did. God sent him on, but only to say exactly what God told him to say.Three Attempts, Three BlessingsBalaam met Balak and explained that a curse on Israel would have to come from Yahweh Himself, since Yahweh was greater than any other god Balak could appeal to. Three times, from three different locations, Balak built altars and set the stage for a curse. Three times, blessing came out of Balaam's mouth instead. God cannot be bribed, pressured, or talked out of what He has already spoken. Each attempt to buy a curse backfired into a deeper blessing, until Balak finally sent Balaam home with no pay and nothing to show for it.A Prophecy Bigger Than MoabBefore Balaam left, four more messages came out of him, this time reaching beyond Israel and Moab. He prophesied a coming King, a star out of Jacob and a scepter out of Israel, who would defeat every nation standing against God's people. Balaam was hired to help Balak defeat Israel. Instead he prophesied Israel's coming King defeating Moab. This is the earliest clear prophecy pointing directly to Jesus Christ as King in the book of Numbers, spoken by a pagan prophet who did not even want to say it.The Real Danger Was Never the CurseBalaam could not curse Israel with words, so later he told Balak a different way to defeat them: draw Israel into idolatry and sexual immorality through the Moabite women. It worked for a time, and thousands of Israelites died, not from a curse spoken over them, but from sin they walked into themselves. What God's character would not be talked into from the outside, sin still accomplished from the inside.Students heard this compared to an athlete who goes undefeated, unbeatable by any opponent, who still loses everything, not to someone else, but to their own choices off the field. No one could hand them the loss. They still handed it to themselves.Paul points back to this exact story in 1 Corinthians 10, telling believers these things happened as examples for us. Israel's protection from outside curses never meant they were safe from compromise from within. Nothing in Christ can undo what God has spoken over a believer. Romans 8 puts it plainly: if God is for us, who can be against us. But that was never the real danger for Israel, and it is not the real danger for us either. The real danger is quietly wandering into compromise that nobody has to force on us.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.Balaam technically never disobeyed God's direct commands. He said exactly what God told him to say each time. So why does the passage still treat him as a villain?Balaam kept trying to find a version of God's will he could negotiate, asking again and hoping for a different answer. Where in your life are you doing the same thing right now, hoping God changes His answer if you just ask in a different way?If nothing can curse someone God has blessed in Christ, why does Paul still bother warning believers in 1 Corinthians 10? What does that tell you about the difference between your security in Christ and your responsibility to walk in it?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Have you ever kept asking a question hoping to get a different answer than the one you already knew?Has a "gut feeling" or a warning from a friend ever kept you from a bad decision? Did you listen right away, or push through it first?What's the difference between someone doing something bad to you and you doing something bad to yourself?Why do you think it's easier to notice a big, obvious danger than a small, quiet compromise?‍

chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuJuly 6, 2025Redemption SeriesCreation: Part 2Liam HungateAbout the SeriesLast week's lesson closed by looking at John 1 and uncovering Jesus' presence and role at creation in Genesis. Tonight built on that, moving into the New Testament to look more closely at Christ's role as both Creator and Redeemer.Passages: Colossians 1-2; 2 Corinthians 4; Hebrews 1; Proverbs 8What Was TaughtCreator, Sustainer, RulerColossians 1:15-16 makes three claims about Christ: everything was created by Him, everything was created through Him, and everything was created for Him. He's not just involved in creation, He's its source and its purpose. The lesson paired this with a few facts meant to inspire genuine wonder: the earth orbits the sun at roughly eight times the speed of a bullet, there are more insects in a single square mile than there are people on the entire planet, and a single human chromosome is said to hold an almost unfathomable amount of genetic information, scaled up across the body's trillions of cells into a staggering total. The point wasn't the numbers themselves, but the reminder that the God who designed all of it isn't a side character in the story.The One Who Holds It All TogetherColossians 1:17-18 says Christ existed before all things and holds all things together. The lesson illustrated this with laminin, a protein in the human body that helps hold cells and tissue together and aids healing, often noted for its cross-like shape. Just as that protein provides physical structure, Jesus provides spiritual and eternal structure. Life spins out of control without Him holding it together.Reconciled Through the CrossColossians 1:19-20 says the fullness of God dwelt in Christ, and through Him, God reconciled everything to Himself through the blood of the cross. The lesson compared Christ's role to a mediator working out peace between two parties, except Christ doesn't just mediate the agreement, He personally pays the cost of it too. God always knew humanity would fall short. Jesus was never a backup plan. He was the plan from eternity.From Alienation to RelationshipColossians 1:21-23 describes believers as once alienated from God, now reconciled through Christ's death. This tied back to Genesis: humanity was formed from dust, separate from God, until His breath brought Adam into relationship with Him. Everyone starts out alienated in the same way, and it's only in receiving God's Spirit that relationship with Him actually begins.Wisdom From the BeginningColossians 2:3 calls Christ the place where all wisdom and knowledge are hidden, which connects to Proverbs 8's picture of "Woman Wisdom" present at creation. Proverbs personifies wisdom and foolishness as two paths people can follow, and Wisdom's own words in Proverbs 8:22-36, describing her presence from before creation, were read alongside Christ's role in the same event, wisdom itself pointing back to Him.The Light That Was Always ThereHebrews 1:2-3 repeats the same themes from Colossians: Christ as Creator, Sustainer, and Ruler, described here as "the radiance of God's glory." That phrase was tied back to Day 1 of creation, where God didn't create light out of nothing so much as reveal light that already existed in Him, since God Himself is light. Picture the universe as a dark, empty canvas with only the Trinity present, and light entering the world as Christ Himself being revealed. Hebrews 1:10-12 reinforces the same point through God's own words to the Son: the earth and heavens will wear out and pass away, but Christ remains, unchanging.Treasure in Jars of Clay2 Corinthians 4:7-12 describes believers as "treasure in jars of clay." The lesson compared this to an empty piggy bank, worthless on its own until it holds something valuable inside. Our ordinary, breakable bodies were designed to carry something priceless: the gospel and the Holy Spirit. Most of us don't feel like treasure, more like something ordinary and a little worn down, but that's exactly the point. God's power shows up through the cracks, not in spite of our ordinariness but through it. Our flesh can be afflicted and even broken down, but the soul stays alive and secure when the Spirit lives inside it.Renewed Day by Day2 Corinthians 4:16-18 promises that even as our outward selves wear down, our inner selves are being renewed daily through the Spirit. The trials along the way, described as "light and momentary afflictions," aren't pointless, they're producing something far weightier and eternal. The call is to stop fixating on what's visible and temporary and to fix attention instead on what's unseen and lasting.A Personal RedeemerChrist holds every one of these massive, cosmic titles, Creator, Sustainer, Ruler of everything that exists. But the closing point was intentionally personal: more than any of those titles, He wants to be the redeemer of your own heart specifically.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.How does Colossians describe Christ's role in creation?According to 2 Corinthians 4, what does it mean to have "treasure in jars of clay"?If Jesus is the Creator, Sustainer, Ruler, and Redeemer, what difference does that make in how you face life's challenges?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:What part of creation makes you feel the most sense of wonder?Do you feel more like an empty piggy bank or a treasure chest most days? Why?What's a "light and momentary" hard season you can look back on now and see some growth from?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuJune 29, 2025Redemption SeriesCreationLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight launched a brand new teaching series called the Redemption Series, kicking off with the newest incoming freshmen at their very first official youth group. It's a long-term project, expected to run somewhere around 70 weeks with breaks along the way for events, Q&A nights, and other topical messages, tracing the story of redemption across the entire Bible rather than staying only in the Gospels. The goal is to help students see how thoroughly the gospel is woven through all of Scripture, starting at Creation, deepening their relationship with God and better equipping them to represent Him well to everyone they meet.Passages: Genesis 1-2; Psalm 19; Job 38; John 1What Was TaughtIn the Beginning, God CreatedGenesis opens with the single clearest statement in the whole Bible: God is the Creator of everything. Before He brought order to it, the earth was empty and dark, with the Spirit of God hovering over the waters, a detail the lesson connected to a pattern that shows up throughout Scripture: the Spirit's presence tends to come right before something good, before redemption. On Day 1, God spoke light into being and separated it from darkness, establishing light as the source of life and darkness as the absence of it.The Sky and the Water Above ItOn Day 2, God separated the water below the sky from water described as being above it. The lesson explained this as a layer of water vapor surrounding the early earth's atmosphere, proposing that it would have created a mild, greenhouse-like global climate with little wind or rain, filtered out harmful radiation, and allowed for the long lifespans recorded in early Genesis, ending only at the flood, when that water is described as falling to the earth.Land, Plants, and Light in the SkyDay 3 brought dry land and the first plant life, notably before the sun existed, meaning the light from Day 1 alone was enough to sustain it. Day 4 introduced the sun, moon, and stars, reinforcing the day-and-night cycle already established and giving humanity a way to track time, seasons, and direction.Every Living Thing According to Its KindDay 5 brought sea creatures and birds, each created "according to their kind." The lesson used dog breeds as an example of built-in variation within a kind, contrasted with the idea that one kind could ever become another. It argued that the fossil record shows no clear transitional evidence between species, and that the odds of life assembling itself from simple chemical building blocks are effectively impossible, compared to a tornado sweeping through a junkyard and accidentally assembling a fully functional airplane.Made in God's ImageDay 6 brought land animals, and then humanity. Genesis 1:26, "let us make man in our image," was pointed to as an early glimpse of the Trinity present at creation. Being made in God's image, the Imago Dei, was taught as what sets humans apart from every other created thing, morally, intellectually, and spiritually, designed to rule creation alongside God as something like co-regents. The first thing God did for Adam and Eve was bless them.A Day of RestOn Day 7, God rested, not out of exhaustion, but to establish a rhythm of rest that's carried down to a seven-day week ever since. The lesson noted that believers today aren't bound to a strict Sabbath law the way Israel once was, since Christ fulfilled that law, but that a regular rhythm of rest and focus on God, the kind many find on a Sunday, still reflects His design. Psalm 19 was read to close this section, as a picture of creation itself declaring God's glory.Evidence for a CreatorThe lesson spent time on arguments against a purely naturalistic origin of life, including doubts about early experiments recreating the chemical conditions of early earth, and statistical arguments about how improbable functioning life is to have formed by chance. It also presented a "fine-tuning" argument: that an enormous number of very specific conditions, from planetary distance and star type to atmospheric composition, all had to align precisely for life to be possible, framed as far too improbable to attribute to chance. DNA itself was described as functioning like a language or code, evidence of a mind behind it rather than pure chemistry. The conclusion drawn: believing life engineered itself actually requires more faith than believing God created it.The Second Telling of Day 6Genesis 2 retells Day 6 in closer detail, not a separate act of creation. Man was formed from dust and given life through God's breath, the Hebrew word used there being closely related to the Hebrew term for the Holy Spirit, meaning God quite literally breathed His own Spirit into Adam. God then planted a garden in Eden and provided everything Adam would need, including four rivers flowing out from it.The Edenic CovenantGod's instructions to Adam formed what the lesson called the Edenic Covenant: made in God's image, ruling over creation, filling the earth, working and watching over the garden, and the one restriction, not eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Notably, Adam was given work to do before sin ever entered the picture, work itself isn't a curse, only the difficulty of it later became one.Not Good to Be AloneGenesis 2 records the first time God calls something not good: man being alone. After Adam named all the animals and found no suitable companion among them, God formed Eve from Adam's rib. The lesson highlighted the placement, not from the foot to be walked over, not from the head to rule over him, but from near the heart and under the arm, symbolizing love and protection. Headship, as taught here, was framed as a call to serve and protect rather than a claim to higher status, alongside a comment that today's culture pushes back against this understanding of gender differences.One FleshGenesis 2:24-25 establishes marriage and family as God's original design, a man leaving his parents to become one flesh with his wife. Adam and Eve, still sinless at this point, felt no shame in their nakedness, since there was nothing yet to hide.Christ Revealed From the BeginningThe lesson closed by turning to John 1 to reveal Christ's presence woven through everything just covered in Genesis, compared to watching a mystery unfold and then seeing the culprit revealed at the end, present the whole time. John 1 identifies Jesus as the Word who was with God from the beginning, through whom everything was created, and the source of the very light introduced on Day 1. John the Baptist came as a witness to that light, though the world, then and now, largely failed to recognize its Creator. Those who do receive Him are given the right to become children of God. The Word became flesh and lived among us, full of grace and truth, distinct from the law given through Moses, and as the only one who has truly revealed the otherwise unseen Father.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.Why is it important to understand God as both Creator and Redeemer?How do these passages enhance our understanding of God's character and His plan for redemption?In what ways does the creation narrative influence our understanding of humanity's role in God's redemptive plan?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:What part of the creation story stood out to you most tonight?Do you find it easier to believe in a Creator when you look at nature, or does it take more thought for you?What does "made in God's image" actually mean to you personally?

chunks.title: Yesterday's Nazism Is Today's Progressivism: Same Snake. Different Skins. | Sermon Notes | The Landmark Church
chunks.text: May 4, 2025Yesterday's Nazism Is Today's Progressivism: Same Snake. Different Skins.The death of definition is the birth of deception.1 John 2:18Little children, it is the last hour; and as you have heard that the Antichrist is coming, even now many antichrists have come, by which we know that it is the last hour.2 Corinthians 11:14For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light.Propaganda and Peddling LiesIf you control the narrative, you can control the nation.2 Thessalonians 2:9-10The coming of the lawless one is according to the working of Satan, with all power, signs, and lying wonders, and with all unrighteous deception among those who perish, because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved.Satan doesn’t just publicize deception; he parades darkness as light and protests truth with lies.Parades and ProtestsVisual spectacle can often overpower rational thought.The spirit of the Antichrist used a swastika in the same way it uses a rainbow.Ephesians 5:11And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather expose them.Parrots and PuppetsThe spirit of Antichrist doesn’t just deceive — it disciples.Scapegoats and SmokescreensThose who refuse to bow must be blamed.Persecution Dressed As Progress“The time is coming that whoever kills you will think that he offers God service.” (John 16:2)When you refuse to bow, you’re no longer called courageous — you’re called dangerous.Discussion QuestionsHow can we discern the spiritual forces behind cultural movements that appear progressive or compassionate on the surface?“Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God; because many false prophets have gone out into the world” (1 John 4:1). “For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14). These verses remind us to exercise spiritual discernment, even when ideologies seem well-meaning or enlightened.In what ways do modern methods of indoctrination resemble those used by totalitarian regimes of the past?“Beware lest anyone cheat you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the basic principles of the world, and not according to Christ” (Colossians 2:8). “For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine… but will turn their ears away from the truth, and be turned aside to fables” (2 Timothy 4:3–4). These warnings show how deception often gains power through repetition and manipulation of truth.What does it look like to stand firm in biblical truth today, especially when it might cost us social approval or personal comfort?“Yes, and all who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3:12). “But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed. And do not be afraid of their threats, nor be troubled” (1 Peter 3:14). Standing firm means accepting the cost of conviction, knowing God honors our faithfulness.How can Christians lovingly expose deception without becoming harsh or reactionary in their response?“But, speaking the truth in love, may grow up in all things into Him who is the head—Christ” (Ephesians 4:15). “And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather expose them” (Ephesians 5:11). These verses encourage a balance of boldness and compassion when confronting falsehood.What does it mean to follow “the King of the Ages” rather than the “spirit of the age,” and how do we live that out practically in daily life?“And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, that you may prove what is that good and acceptable and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2). Faithful living means setting our sights on God’s eternal truth rather than temporary cultural trends.

chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuApril 12, 2026Redemption SeriesExodusLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight returned to Exodus, picking up with Moses as a shepherd in Midian after fleeing Egypt. Quick refresher: Moses was born while Pharaoh had ordered every Israelite baby boy killed, was placed in a basket on the river, and was found and raised inside Pharaoh's own household, all while wrestling with whether he belonged with the Egyptians or the Israelites.The lesson opened by imagining the kind of elaborate, meticulously planned escape it would take to break just one person out of a high-security prison, every move calculated, everything depending on human effort. Then it scaled that up: not one person, but millions, set free not through planning or effort, but purely through God orchestrating every step.Passages: Exodus 3, 12-15; Psalm 136What Was TaughtA Reluctant RescuerGod called Moses through a burning bush on Mount Horeb, the same mountain where His presence shows up again and again through Exodus. God had heard the cries of His enslaved people and was ready to act, choosing Moses to lead them out. Moses' response was to ask, "Who am I to do this?" And he wasn't wrong, he wasn't worthy. But the point isn't our worthiness. It's what God wants to do through us. God answered simply: "I will certainly be with you," promising that Israel would one day return to this very mountain, free and worshiping.The Great I AmGiven his track record, Moses wanted credentials before going back to confront Pharaoh. God gave him His name: I AM WHO I AM, Yahweh, rendered as "LORD" in all capital letters throughout the Old Testament. It's a name that points to God being eternal and self-existing, simply and always is. With that name behind him, Moses had everything he needed, along with a warning that Egypt wouldn't let Israel go easily.PassoverAfter ten plagues broke Pharaoh's resistance, the final one, Passover, sealed it. God warned that He would pass through Egypt and take the firstborn son of every household, but offered Israel a way out: sacrifice a lamb and paint its blood on the doorposts, and death would pass over that home. A life given on behalf of others made forgiveness possible, and God wanted this night remembered permanently, with the same posture of gratitude and remembrance that should mark how we live in response to being saved. Pharaoh, finally broken after all he'd endured, let Israel go and even asked Moses for a blessing from the God he had spent so long defying.Free at Last, Guided by GodSomewhere around two to three million Israelites walked out of Egypt after 430 years of captivity. God didn't just lead them through Moses, He was physically present with them, a cloud covering and guiding them by day and a pillar of fire lighting the way by night, described as the original GPS. He deliberately routed them away from war and opposition, protection they likely never fully realized was happening.Freedom didn't mean the danger was over. Just days into the journey, Pharaoh changed his mind and pursued them with his army. Trapped between the sea and the approaching Egyptians, with no weapons and nowhere to run, Israel was terrified. That trapped feeling was the point: it's often not the big things we already know only God can handle that trip us up, but the smaller things we think we can manage on our own.Through the SeaWith the Egyptians closing in, God split the sea and Israel crossed on dry ground with walls of water on either side, one of the greatest miracles in Scripture. There was no plan or fighting involved, only faith in a God who rescues, the way a lifeguard pulls in someone who's been swept out too far. Exodus is a small picture of the larger freedom God wants to give: freedom and protection from sin, death, and the enemy. When the pursuing Egyptian army followed them into the sea, the waters closed over them, and Israel responded with a song of praise, exactly the posture of gratitude we're meant to carry for our own rescue.His Love Endures ForeverThe night closed in Psalm 136, a psalm built entirely around the refrain that God's love endures forever. Where do you feel stuck right now, like there's no way out? What are you trying to fix or manage on your own instead of trusting God with it, whether that's anxiety, a struggling relationship, or something you've tried to fix over and over? The same God who rescued Israel at the Red Sea is the only one who can rescue you too.Coming Up Next WeekA closer look at the ten plagues that led up to this moment.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.Why did God lead the Israelites into a situation where they were trapped between the Red Sea and the Egyptians?How is the Exodus story similar to what Jesus has done for us?Has there ever been a time in your life where you know what God has done for you in the past, yet you still find yourself doubting in the future?What is something in your life right now that you're trying to handle on your own instead of trusting God with it? What would it look like for you to actually trust Him in that situation?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Have you ever felt trapped with no way out, and then things worked out in a way you didn't expect?What's something small you try to handle on your own instead of asking for help?What does it look like for you to say thank you to God after something goes right?

chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuSeptember 13, 2026Redemption SeriesGideon's ArmyLiam HungatePassages: Judges 6-8This week in the Redemption Series, students picked up in the book of Judges, right after the story of Joshua. Israel had just been challenged to choose who they would serve, and they answered by turning to false gods almost immediately. That sets up a repeating cycle in Judges: Israel sins, God hands them over to an enemy, Israel cries out, God raises up a leader called a judge to rescue them, there is peace for a while, the judge dies, and the cycle starts again.‍What Was TaughtMeet GideonBefore Gideon, four other judges kept Israel afloat: Othniel, Ehud, Shamgar, and Deborah. Each time, even though Israel kept falling into sin, God still rescued His people. By Gideon's time, Israel was being crushed by Midian, who raided their land every harvest and destroyed their crops and livestock. Israel cried out, and God sent His angel to a man named Gideon, hiding from the enemy, and called him a "mighty warrior."Gideon did not feel like one. He doubted God out loud, asking where all the wonders his ancestors talked about had gone, and told God that his family was the weakest in their tribe and he was the least in his family. God did not argue with him. He simply told Gideon that He would be with him.A faith that needed confirmationGideon asked God for sign after sign before he would move: an offering consumed by fire, then a wool fleece soaked with dew while the ground stayed dry, then the same fleece dry while the ground around it was wet. God patiently gave him each one. Gideon's faith was weak, but it was still faith, and God met him in it rather than shaming him for it.Gideon also obeyed God's first hard instruction, tearing down the town's altar to Baal, but he did it at night, afraid of how his family and neighbors would react. God was clearly still building Gideon's courage step by step.An army shrunk on purpose32,000 down to 300. God trimmed Gideon's army twice so that when the battle was won, no one could claim Israel had saved itself.Courage and alertness. The men God kept were the ones willing to fight and the ones who stayed watchful for the enemy, a picture of how believers are called to live today.With just 300 men, Gideon overheard an enemy soldier describe a dream about a loaf of bread flattening a tent, which a fellow soldier interpreted as Gideon's coming victory. That was enough to settle Gideon's confidence for the fight ahead. God's plan threw the massive Midianite camp into chaos in the dark, and the enemy turned on itself and fled.Finishing what God startedMost people would have stopped once the enemy camp scattered. Gideon and his exhausted 300 kept going, chasing down two Midianite kings who had killed his own brothers, and finished the mission completely. When Israel then asked Gideon to rule over them, he refused, saying the Lord would rule over Israel, not him. After everything Gideon had accomplished, he still pointed back to God instead of himself.A blind spot at the endIsrael had 40 years of peace under Gideon, but a gift he gave Israel after the victory later became something Israel worshiped in his place, and the nation slid right back into idolatry after his death. Even one of the best judges Israel ever had could not fix what was broken in Israel's heart. That is the whole point of the Judges cycle: Israel did not need a rescuer for a season. They needed a King who would never fail them and never leave them to fall apart again, which is exactly what Jesus is.‍Talk About It at HomeThese are the questions students were asked tonight. Use one or two, not all four:Have you ever felt like you were the "least likely" or least qualified person for something you were a part of? What did you do with that?God intentionally shrunk Gideon's army so no one could take credit but Him. Is there an area of your life right now where you're tempted to take credit for something that was really God's doing?Gideon and his men finished the job instead of stopping at "good enough." Where in your own life have you stopped short of finishing something God had placed in your life? What would it look like to go back and see it through to the finish line?Where might your words be pointing people toward God while something else you're doing is quietly pointing them somewhere else?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:If God asked you to do something and gave you three chances to double check it was really Him, would you feel silly asking, or relieved He was patient with you?Who is someone you know who does a hard thing well but stays humble about it?What is a "blind spot" you check for when you're driving? What would a blind spot in someone's faith look like?Is there a job or responsibility you've had that you finished all the way through, even after it got hard or boring?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuSeptember 14, 2025Redemption SeriesGod's Promise: Part 2Liam HungateAbout the SeriesLast week covered Abraham's story in depth: his covenant with God, the birth of Ishmael, his renaming, the judgment of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the birth and testing of Isaac. The big takeaway was that righteousness comes by faith, not perfection, and that God keeps His promises no matter how long it takes. Tonight picked up there and traced that same promise forward into the New Testament.Passages: Matthew 1:1-17; Romans 4; Galatians 3What Was TaughtA Family Line Built on Grace, Not PerfectionThe New Testament opens with Jesus' genealogy in Matthew 1, deliberately placing Him front and center from the very first verse and tying Him directly to God's promises to both Abraham and David. Matthew, writing primarily to a Jewish audience, needed to show Jesus was a genuine descendant of David to fulfill the Messianic prophecy, and Jewish genealogical records of the time were kept carefully enough that no one seriously disputed the accuracy of what he presented.The genealogy runs in three stretches, Abraham to David, David to the exile, and the exile to Jesus, and includes four women, unusual for genealogies of that era: Tamar, who fought to protect her family line after the deaths of her first two husbands; Rahab, a prostitute in Jericho who protected Israelite spies and chose faithfulness to God over her own government; Ruth, whose loyalty to her mother-in-law reflected the faithfulness God calls His people to; and Bathsheba, referred to as Uriah's wife, whose story with David involved real sin but also real repentance. The point: Jesus' family line was never made up of perfect people, royalty, or wealth. It included sin and poverty, which is exactly the kind of people He spent His life serving.Two Lines, One Claim to the ThroneMatthew 1:16 is careful to say Joseph was "the husband of Mary," not Jesus' father, since there was no blood relation between them. That raises a fair question: why trace Joseph's lineage rather than Mary's? Both Joseph and Mary descend from David, but through different sons, Joseph through Solomon and Mary through Nathan. Solomon's line carried the legal claim to David's throne, but it also carried a curse through a later king, Jeconiah, disqualifying his biological descendants from ever ruling. Because Jesus isn't Joseph's biological son, He bypasses that curse entirely while still holding a legitimate legal claim to the throne through Joseph, and a direct blood connection to David through Mary. It's a level of detail that shows just how deliberately God kept His word across many, many generations. One of the leaders shared a personal note here too, about having no family history in Christianity and God moving him across the country before revealing Himself to him afterward, a small picture of the same kind of intentional pursuit.Credited, Not EarnedRomans 4 points back to Abraham as the model of faith, quoting Genesis 15:6: Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness. Being made right with God was never about Abraham's works, only his belief, and that same righteousness is offered to us as a gift, credited to our account rather than earned. Work expects payment as something owed. Faith simply receives what's freely given. The lesson illustrated the difference between justice, mercy, and grace using a soccer example: justice is running sprints for showing up late, mercy is running fewer sprints than deserved, and grace is skipping the punishment altogether and getting to play a favorite game instead. None of it can be earned, which is exactly the point.The Promise Extended to All Who BelieveBecause the promise comes by faith rather than the law, it's guaranteed not just to Abraham's physical descendants, but to everyone who shares his faith, making him the father of all who believe. Abraham's faith never wavered, even considering how old he and Sarah were when Isaac was finally born. Romans 4 closes by saying that same crediting of righteousness wasn't just for Abraham, it's for anyone who believes in the God who raised Jesus from the dead, since Jesus was handed over for our sins and raised to secure our justification.Heirs to the PromiseGalatians 3 picks up the same thread: those who have faith are Abraham's true sons. Scripture had already announced the gospel to Abraham in advance, that all nations would be blessed through him, meaning the gospel was never limited to the Jewish people alone. Through faith, believers become children of God, clothed with Christ through baptism, with none of the old dividing lines, Jew or Greek, slave or free, male or female, carrying any weight anymore. Belonging to Christ is what makes someone an heir of the promise given to Abraham.Where This Leaves UsThis ancient promise still plays out today, not just through Abraham's and David's family lines or Christ's earthly ministry, but through Christ's Spirit living in believers now. The only real question that matters is whether or not you belong to Christ, not whether you're a good person, what church background you come from, your gender, or your financial situation. Belonging to Him settles our future, since we're children of God, our present, since we're family to every other believer, and our place in a much bigger story, since we're heirs playing a role in God's plan of redemption.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.What important people are in Matthew's genealogy for Jesus, and why is this significant for God's promise to Abraham?What is the difference between being justified by works and being justified by faith, like we talked about in Romans 4?If faith, not works, is what makes us right with God, how should that change the way you approach your relationship with Him?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Do you ever feel like you have to prove you're "good enough" to be loved, by God or by other people?Has anyone in your family history surprised you, in a good or hard way, once you learned more about them?What would change for you if you really believed grace can't be earned?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuAugust 23, 2026Redemption SeriesDeath of MosesLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight closed out a major stretch of the Redemption Series: the Pentateuch. Students spent the last several weeks moving through Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers, and tonight finished Deuteronomy with the last four chapters of Moses' life.Passages: Deuteronomy 30:19-20, 31:6-8, 32:7-18, 32:46-47, 33:26-29, 34, 18:15What Was TaughtThe Choice Before IsraelMoses stood at the edge of the Promised Land, 120 years old, knowing he would not enter it. Before his final words, he laid out a clear choice for Israel: life or death, blessing or curse. Choosing life meant loving God, obeying His voice, and following Him. It was not a vague feeling. It was a direct call to choose God Himself.Passing the Baton to JoshuaMoses turned to Joshua and to the whole nation and repeated a now-famous charge: be strong, be courageous, do not be afraid, because God goes with you and will never leave you. After forty years leading Israel, Moses did not point to himself or to Joshua's ability. He pointed to God's presence.Students heard this compared to a relay race. The runner finishing a leg does not hand off the baton and walk away. He runs alongside the next runner for a few strides to make sure the handoff is clean. That is what Moses was doing: making sure God's presence and promise passed cleanly into the next generation's hands before he stepped off the track.The Song of MosesIn Chapter 32, Moses wrote Israel a song so the truth would live in their memory long after he was gone. The song pictures God as an eagle stirring up its nest, catching a falling Israel and carrying it to safety. Students heard this compared to a parent teaching a child to swim: the child is learning and growing, but there is a steady hand under them the whole time.The song then turns. Israel, even when faithful, kept growing comfortable and complacent. They complained about and forgot the God who made them, trading Him for gods they had invented. Students heard this compared to a kid whose parents worked two jobs to pay for his cleats and never missed a game, who then gets embarrassed to be seen with them once he makes varsity. Nothing changed about what the parents did. He just got comfortable enough to forget it mattered. Israel got comfortable enough to stop noticing God's provision, not because it stopped.The song lands on one line: these are not idle words, they are our life. Follow the God who saves, heals, and restores, and remember what happens to those who desert Him.Consequence and BlessingAfter the song, God told Moses to climb a mountain and view the Promised Land from a distance, because that was as close as he would get. This was the consequence for striking the rock instead of speaking to it back in Numbers, and taking credit that belonged to God. Even in his final moments, the text does not soften that consequence. Moses led faithfully for forty years and still did not get to walk in.Even so, Moses' final words to Israel were not another warning. They were a blessing: there is no one like the God of Israel, who rides the heavens to help His people, whose eternal arms are underneath them. Israel is blessed and secure because of who God is, not because of anything they had done.The Death of MosesThe Pentateuch closes in Chapter 34 with three things worth noting. First, Moses saw the Promised Land but did not enter it. Even the man who spoke with God face to face fell short of the goal he spent his life working toward. Second, God buried him personally, and no one knows where. Moses' story does not end with a monument he built for himself. It ends in God's hands. Third, the text says no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses, since, pointing back to Moses' own words in Deuteronomy 18:15 promising a prophet still to come. The door was not closed. It was being held open.Where This PointsMoses, the most faithful man of his generation, still could not get God's people all the way home. That means whoever does has to be greater than him. Where Moses could only lead people to the edge of the promise, Jesus actually walks His people all the way in. Where Moses died with the job unfinished, Jesus said "it is finished" and meant it. Moses spent his last words telling Israel to choose life. Jesus is the life, and He is still saying the same thing tonight.Students also heard a picture from the courtroom: a hung jury cannot set anyone free. If a jury cannot reach a verdict, the case does not just go away. It stays unresolved. Not deciding was never neutral. It only delays the weight of the decision. There is no undecided seat with Jesus. Not choosing Him already is a choice.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.Israel got "fat" and comfortable and fought against the God who protected them. Where in your life right now are you the most comfortable, and is that comfort making you more grateful to God, or less aware of Him?The second generation of Israel never personally experienced Sinai or the Red Sea. Everything they knew about God came secondhand, passed down from someone else. Who in your life has passed down your understanding of who God is? Have you actually made it your own, or are you still running on borrowed faith?We talked about the quote: "Not to choose to accept is to choose to reject. To do nothing is to choose death." Why do you think so many people treat "I haven't decided yet about Jesus" as a safe, neutral place to stand? What would you say to someone who thinks staying undecided costs them nothing?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:If you could hear one more thing from someone you love before they died, what would you want it to be?What's something you were taught by a parent, coach, or teacher that you didn't appreciate until later?Have you ever avoided making a decision because it felt easier than choosing? What happened?What's one thing about God you know because someone else told you about Him, rather than something you experienced yourself?‍
