chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuMay 24, 2026Redemption SeriesDwelling PlaceLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight continued the Redemption Series through the middle of Exodus, picking up as Israel arrived at the foot of Mount Sinai and God began laying out His Law. The lesson opened around one question that runs through the whole Old Testament: God is holy, we are sinful, so how could the two ever be close? The picture used to frame it: a parent crossing the distance to reach a child who was still running away, rather than waiting for the child to find their own way back. That's the shape of everything covered tonight.Passages: Exodus 19-20, 24, 34, 40; Leviticus 16What Was TaughtRescued First, Then Given the LawBy the time Israel reached Sinai, three months after leaving Egypt, they had crossed the Red Sea, eaten bread from heaven, drawn water from a rock, and won a battle. God described His care for them in Exodus 19:4 using the image of an eagle: eagles are known to carry their young on their backs rather than in their claws, so that any threat from below would have to go through the mother first. God's purpose in rescuing Israel wasn't just to set them free. It was to bring them into fellowship with Him.God then gave the Ten Commandments aloud to the whole nation at the foot of the mountain:No other gods before HimNo worship of idols or carved imagesDon't use the Lord's name in vainRemember the Sabbath dayHonor your parentsDon't murderDon't commit adulteryDon't stealDon't give false testimonyDon't covetThese commandments serve as the foundation of the Law, which does three things: it's a guardrail that keeps us on a moral path, a mirror that shows our failure and need for a savior, and a guide that reveals the heart and desire of God for His people. The order matters: God rescued Israel first, then gave them the Law. It was never a bar Israel had to clear to earn His love. It was instruction for a people He had already claimed. Every believer since has needed the same thing Israel did: someone who could keep that Law perfectly, since we can't. That's exactly what Jesus came to do (Matthew 5:17).A Covenant Sealed in BloodExodus 24 marks the start of the Mosaic Covenant, distinct from the earlier covenant God made with Abraham. This one wasn't about new promises. It formally established that cleansing sin would require a sacrifice, the shedding of blood. Sin carries a real cost, paid for with another life. In the Old Testament that meant repeated animal sacrifices. In the New Testament, Christ gave Himself once, for good.The Same God, Yesterday and TodayBy Exodus 34, Israel had already broken this new covenant. Rather than destroying them, God revealed His own character to Moses: compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in love, with judgment reserved for those who reject that love and forgiveness. There is no angry Old Testament God who is somehow different from the God of the New Testament. He is the same, loving and merciful, yesterday, today, and forever.God Moves InExodus 40 closes the book with the completed Tabernacle, and when it was finished, God's glory filled it, the same presence that had rested on Sinai now dwelling among His people. God has never been distant. Building Him a home wasn't about high maintenance, it was about His desire to be close. John 1:14 later says the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us, using a Greek word that literally means "to tabernacle." The Tabernacle in Exodus was a preview of Christ Himself coming to dwell with us.The Day of AtonementWith a holy God now present among sinful people, ongoing atonement, making amends for wrongdoing, was necessary. Leviticus 16 lays out the yearly Day of Atonement, when the high priest followed three steps: sacrifice a bull for his own sin, sacrifice one goat for the sins of the people, and release a second goat, the scapegoat, into the wilderness carrying the people's sins away. The first goat shows how atonement is granted, through the sacrificial payment of another life. The second shows its effect, sin carried far away and not returning.One way of picturing it: backing your parents' car into something you can't afford to fix, and instead of making you pay, they simply cover it themselves. The damage doesn't disappear and neither does the cost, someone else just absorbs it. That's atonement. In the Old Testament, that cost was paid by an animal. Ultimately, it was paid by Jesus, who serves as the High Priest, the sacrificial lamb, and the scapegoat all at once, suffering to make His people holy through His own blood (Hebrews 13:12).Where This PointsThe question stands the same today: how can a holy God dwell with sinful people? The gap hasn't gotten smaller. But the solution is no longer a mountain we can't climb, a room we can't enter, or an animal we have to sacrifice. The solution is a person, and He's already done the work. The job now isn't to earn acceptance or make up for sin through effort. It's to receive what's already been provided, and to live like someone who is already loved, no matter how many times we fall down.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.When Israel broke the covenant almost immediately, God's first response was to reveal His mercy and compassion. Does that surprise you? What did you expect His response to be, and what does the actual response tell you about who He is?The Israelites had to go through this entire process every single year. It never stuck permanently. How does that make you feel about what Jesus did once and for all?Where in your life do you feel the most distance from God? What do you think creates that gap for you personally?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Have you ever felt like you had to "earn" someone's love before you could relax around them?What's something someone else paid for on your behalf, even though you were the one who messed up?What does it look like for you to feel close to God versus far from Him?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuApril 26, 2026Redemption SeriesExodus: Part 2Liam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight was a follow-up to the lesson from two weeks ago on Moses' call and Israel's rescue through the Red Sea. Rather than staying inside Exodus, the group stepped out to see how far God's heart for His people actually reaches, tracing a thread from a minor prophet centuries later all the way to the cross.The lesson opened with a picture of choosing to love someone who's genuinely hard to love, someone chaotic, someone who keeps pushing people away, and refusing to give up on them anyway. That's the same way God feels about us, and tonight was about how He proved it.Passages: Hosea 11; Matthew 2, 26What Was TaughtA Father Who Can't Give Up on His SonHosea, one of the Minor Prophets, wrote roughly 500 years after the Exodus, and God's love for Israel hadn't faded. Hosea 11 opens with God recalling how He called His son out of Egypt, then moves into Israel's ongoing struggle with idolatry, and God's gentle, easily overlooked care for His people all along, the kind of care a newborn receives without ever realizing how much is being done for it.The chapter turns toward Israel's stubborn unbelief, yet God says, "How can I give you up?" naming two cities, Admah and Zeboiim, that were destroyed alongside Sodom and Gomorrah in Genesis. Justice demands that sin be paid for. But even facing a people who deserved judgment, God's heart searched for a way to save them instead of destroy them. That way was Jesus, who was "given up" on the cross in Israel's place, and in ours.Out of EgyptHosea 11:1, "out of Egypt I called my son," is quoted directly in Matthew 2 and applied to Jesus. After His birth, wise men set out to find Him, which alarmed King Herod, who saw the newborn as a threat to his throne. A prophecy from Micah, another minor prophet, confirmed where the Messiah would be found. Herod told the wise men to report back so he could "worship" Jesus, but he actually intended to kill Him. Warned in a dream, the wise men avoided Herod entirely, and Joseph, warned as well, immediately took his family to Egypt to escape Herod's threat.After Herod's death, God called the family back to Israel, where they settled in Nazareth, fulfilling Hosea's centuries-old words. What looked like a small detail in the Christmas story was actually the same rescue pattern from Exodus playing out again, this time around God's own Son.A Meal Before the SacrificeFast forward to Matthew 26, where Jesus, fully aware His suffering was coming and necessary, not optional, prepared His disciples for what was ahead. He hosted the Passover meal, the very meal that celebrated Israel's deliverance from Egypt, in an upper room, described as something like a final meal shared with family before someone leaves for deployment. There, He offered Himself as the sacrifice that would replace the Exodus as the central act of redemption, this time centered on Himself rather than a nation walking out of slavery.Obedient to the EndIn the Garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prayed for another way if one existed, while ultimately submitting to God's will, because salvation could not come any other way without His death being unnecessary. When the chief priests came to arrest Him, He didn't resist, even though He had the power to stop it entirely. Picture someone with overwhelming power simply letting themselves be taken. That's not powerlessness, it's purpose. Jesus knew exactly what needed to happen and chose it anyway.The GospelNone of this was deserved. Israel was actively turning from God even as He affirmed His love for them, and we fall short of Him daily in the same way. That's exactly the depth of His love: Christ's obedience makes up for where we fail, because all God wants is to be in a right relationship with us. Redemption is fulfilled through Jesus' sacrifice. By His blood, we're saved, and all that's asked of us is to believe it.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.How would you describe God's heart toward Israel in your own words? Why was it necessary for Jesus to go to the cross?God loved Israel even while they were actively turning their backs on Him. Does that change how you think about what you have to do to "earn" God's love?What's one area of your life you've been keeping from Him because you don't feel worthy?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Has anyone ever kept loving you even when you were hard to love? What was that like?Do you feel like you have to be "good" before you can come to God, or after?What's something you're hiding or holding back from God right now?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuNovember 16, 2025Redemption SeriesJosephLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight closed out the book of Genesis with the final of its eight "stepping stones": Creation, Fall, Flood, Tower, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and now Joseph. Where Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob each had to learn to trust God's promise in their own way, tonight showed Joseph learning that same lesson through one of the most dramatic stories in the Bible.Passages: Genesis 37-50What Was TaughtSold by His BrothersJoseph was 17, the second-youngest of twelve brothers, and clearly his father Jacob's favorite, which bred deep jealousy among his brothers. When Jacob shared two dreams Joseph had, both picturing his family bowing down to him, the brothers had had enough and plotted to kill him. Reuben talked them into trapping him instead, planning to rescue him quietly later, but before he could, the other brothers sold Joseph to a group of traders heading to Egypt. Reuben returned to find Joseph gone. To cover their tracks, the brothers dipped Joseph's coat in goat's blood and let Jacob believe his son had been killed by an animal.Judah's Hidden SinAs Joseph is taken to Egypt, the story briefly shifts to his brother Judah, showing that God was working through more than one story at once. Judah's oldest son married a woman named Tamar and was struck down by God for wickedness. By custom, the next son was to marry Tamar to continue his brother's family line, but he too was struck down. Judah wrongly blamed Tamar and refused to give her his third son as custom required. Later, not recognizing her, Judah slept with a veiled Tamar, believing she was a prostitute, and she became pregnant. When he learned of the pregnancy, Judah ordered her execution, until Tamar revealed the truth: it was his child. Judah repented openly, acknowledging his wrong in both matters. Tamar gave birth to twins, and through one of them, Perez, God preserved the family line that would eventually lead to David, and to Jesus. Two stories ran side by side here, one of repentance, one of faithfulness, both part of the same larger plan.Faithful in Slavery, Faithful in PrisonIn Egypt, Joseph was bought by Potiphar, one of Pharaoh's officials, who came to trust him so completely that he handed Joseph full control of his household. Potiphar's wife tried repeatedly to seduce him, and when Joseph refused, she falsely accused him, landing him in prison. Even there, God gave Joseph favor, and he was put in charge of the other prisoners. Two of them, Pharaoh's former baker and cupbearer, had troubling dreams that Joseph correctly interpreted, one predicting restoration, the other execution. The cupbearer, restored to his position, forgot about Joseph for two full years.From Prisoner to PrinceWhen Pharaoh himself had a disturbing dream no one could interpret, the cupbearer finally remembered Joseph. Joseph explained that the dream pointed to seven years of abundance followed by seven years of famine, and offered a plan to prepare for it. Pharaoh recognized God's hand on Joseph and made him second-in-command over all of Egypt, giving him fine clothing, a home, a wife, and two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. Joseph oversaw the storage of food during the years of plenty, and when famine hit, Egypt had more than enough, enough that people came from all over the world to buy grain from Joseph himself.Testing and ReconciliationAmong those who came to buy grain were Joseph's own brothers, who didn't recognize the powerful Egyptian official standing before them. Before revealing himself, Joseph tested their character, requiring them to return with their youngest brother Benjamin while keeping Simeon behind as collateral. Jacob, already having lost one son, was reluctant to risk Benjamin as well. But Judah, changed by what he'd learned through his own failures, took personal responsibility for Benjamin's safety. When Joseph tested them again by threatening to keep Benjamin as a slave, Judah offered himself in his brother's place instead. Seeing that same transformation, Joseph finally revealed who he really was, and the brothers reconciled.You Meant It for Evil, God Meant It for GoodJoseph didn't blame his brothers for what they'd done. He recognized that every hard turn in his story, sold into slavery, falsely accused, imprisoned, forgotten, had positioned him exactly where he needed to be to save many lives during the famine. Looking back over the whole arc, sold by his brothers, elevated by Potiphar, falsely accused, imprisoned, elevated again by Pharaoh, and finally the one who saved Egypt and his own family, it's a story built entirely out of highs and lows redeemed. When Jacob learned Joseph was alive, he came to Egypt immediately for an emotional reunion, and Pharaoh provided generously for Joseph's whole family, giving them a home and favor in the land.A Final BlessingBefore he died, Jacob blessed Joseph's two sons, and in a pattern echoing his own reversal over his older brother Esau, declared that the younger son, Ephraim, would be greater than the firstborn, Manasseh. After blessing his sons, Jacob died.Forgiveness in AbundanceIn the mourning that followed, Joseph reassured his brothers with the words the whole story has been building toward: what they intended for evil, God intended for good, to save many lives. God can take our failures and mistakes and use them for His purposes. Joseph didn't stop at forgiveness either. He provided for his brothers in abundance, the same way God, despite how often we fall short, offers not just forgiveness through His own Son but blessing on top of it. Like a child in timeout who would gladly accept an early release the moment it's offered, we're often the ones who hesitate, knowing forgiveness is available and still not fully believing or receiving it. A gift offered at the door still has to be opened to do any good.Where This PointsGenesis closes with Joseph's death, and his final words point forward: a reassurance that God would one day bring His people out of Egypt and into the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. That's exactly where the story picks up next.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.What does Joseph mean when he says, "You meant it for evil, but God meant it for good"?How do Joseph and Judah both change from the beginning of their stories to the end? How are they similar, and how are they different?Joseph waited years in slavery and prison before seeing God's plan. How do you respond when it feels like God is taking too long?Joseph's brothers struggled to believe they were forgiven. Do you ever struggle to believe God really forgives you? Why?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Has something bad ever happened to you that ended up leading to something good later?Is it easier for you to forgive someone else, or to believe you've actually been forgiven yourself?What's something you're still waiting on right now that's testing your patience?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuSeptember 6, 2026Redemption SeriesJoshuaLiam HungatePassages: Joshua 1-2, 6, 23-24; Deuteronomy 1-3This week in the Redemption Series, students moved from the end of Deuteronomy into the book of Joshua. Moses had just closed out his final words to Israel with a choice: life or death, blessing or curse, and Israel would spend the rest of its story answering that choice one generation at a time. Moses was not allowed to lead Israel into the Promised Land himself. That job went to Joshua, one of only two spies who had trusted God enough to say Canaan could actually be taken. What Was TaughtA new leader, ready or notJoshua stepped into leadership right after Moses died, and God's first words to him were not a strategy, they were a command: be strong and courageous. Joshua had watched Moses talk with God face to face, and it is easy to imagine him feeling unqualified to follow that. God did not remove Joshua's fear. He asked for obedience anyway, and Joshua's willingness to seek and surrender to God became the thing that carried him forward.Rahab and the spiesBefore Israel moved on Jericho, Joshua sent two spies into the city. Rahab, a prostitute living in the city wall, hid them from soldiers because she and the rest of Jericho had already heard what God had done for Israel and feared Him. In exchange for protecting the spies, she asked for her family to be spared when Israel attacked, marked by a scarlet cord tied in her window. Her story is proof that even someone completely outside Israel could recognize and respond to God's power.The fall of JerichoGod told Joshua the city was already as good as won, then gave him a battle plan that looked nothing like a battle: march around the city, blow trumpets, and shout. Jericho was Canaan's most fortified city, and Israel's only weapon was obedience. On the seventh day, after marching in silence for six, the walls came down exactly as promised.Faith. Israel believed an unusual plan because it came from God.Obedience. They followed the instructions exactly as given.Courage. They marched with no defense and stayed vulnerable the whole time.Endurance. They kept going even when nothing seemed to be happening.Trust. Their confidence was in the Lord, not in themselves.Finishing what God startedJericho was only the first of many battles as Israel moved through the south and north of Canaan. Some victories came easily, others took real fighting, and Israel got it wrong at least once, disobeying God at Ai and paying for it before God corrected and moved them forward again. Scripture later stops to summarize that God gave Israel the land and kept every promise He made, but that did not mean the work was finished. Some tribes pressed in and claimed what was theirs. Others got comfortable and left the job half done, a decision that would cost them later.Joshua's final challengeNear the end of his life, Joshua gathered Israel one last time and retold their whole story, repeating "I gave, I gave, I did" to make sure they knew every bit of it was God's doing, not theirs. Then he handed the decision back to them: choose who you will serve. Israel answered that they would serve the Lord, and Joshua made a covenant with them as a witness to that promise. Not long after, he died and was buried in the very land God had promised to give them. Talk About It at HomeThese are the questions students were asked tonight. Use one or two, not all three:Like Joshua looked back at Israel's whole story, take a minute to look back at yours. Where has God already been faithful to you, even if you didn't notice it at the time?Even after everything God had done, some tribes still didn't finish the job. Why do you think it's possible to believe God kept His promises and still not fully obey Him? Is there something God has called you to that you've gotten comfortable leaving unfinished?"As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord." If you said that and meant it, what would actually have to change this week?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Has there ever been a time you had to lead or step up even though you didn't feel ready?What's something that seemed impossible that turned out fine once you actually tried it?Is there something you've started and never quite finished?If you had to say out loud who or what you're serving right now, what would it be?‍

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuSeptember 7, 2025Redemption SeriesGod's PromiseLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight moved the Redemption Series from the Tower of Babel into the story of Abraham, the next of Genesis' major figures. After Babel, God scattered a rebellious humanity and began looking for a new remnant, a faithful man to start a new covenant with. That man was Abram.Passages: Genesis 12-22What Was TaughtA Promise RepeatedAbram, whose name means "high father," was married to Sarai, "my princess," and the two were childless, an irony given his name. God called Abram to leave his land, his relatives, and his father's house for a land God would show him, promising to make him into a great nation, to bless him, to make his name great, to bless those who blessed him and curse those who treated him with contempt, and that all the peoples on earth would be blessed through him, ultimately through the Savior who would come from his line.This wasn't actually the first time Abram heard this promise. He'd received it earlier, before moving to Haran, but hadn't fully obeyed. Only after his father died did Abram move toward fuller obedience, prompting God to repeat the promise. Abram isn't presented as a finished example of faith from the start. He's presented as someone growing into it, much like us.Partial Obedience, Real ConsequencesEven in obeying, Abram brought along his nephew Lot, despite being told to leave his relatives behind. When he arrived in the promised land, the Canaanites were already living there and had no intention of leaving. Then a famine hit, and instead of trusting God to provide where he was, Abram went down to Egypt. It's often easier to trust God for far-off promises than for today's actual needs.In Egypt, fearing for his life, Abram told everyone Sarai was his sister rather than his wife. Pharaoh took her into his household, and God struck Pharaoh's house with plagues to protect Sarai, since the Messiah's line would come through her. Even in the middle of Abram's failure, God protected His own promise. Abram and Lot eventually returned to Canaan, but the land couldn't support both of their growing households, so they separated, and Lot unknowingly settled near a deeply sinful population, a decision that would matter later.The Gospel in a PromiseIn Genesis 15, God came to Abram in a vision telling him not to be afraid, that God Himself was his shield and reward. Abram, still childless, pushed back, wondering if his servant would end up his heir by default. God clarified that a biological son was coming, and that Abram's descendants would be as numerous as the stars, one of whom would ultimately be the Messiah Himself. Genesis 15:6 records Abram's response: he believed the Lord, and it was credited to him as righteousness, the first mention of both belief and righteousness in the Bible, and essentially the gospel in miniature this early in the Old Testament. God then formally established His covenant with Abram, laying out the specific boundaries of the land his descendants would inherit, what Scripture would come to call the Promised Land.Hagar and IshmaelStill waiting on the promised son, Sarai grew impatient and gave her servant Hagar to Abram to build a family through her instead. Once Hagar became pregnant, tension between the two women grew so severe that Hagar fled. An angel met her and told her to return and submit to Sarai, promising that her offspring would also be greatly multiplied. She named her son Ishmael, meaning "God hears," though the angel's accompanying prophecy, that his hand would be against everyone and everyone's hand against him, wasn't an easy one to carry.New Names, a Coming SonIn Genesis 17, God renewed His covenant further, renaming Abram to Abraham, "father of many nations," and Sarai to Sarah, and instituting circumcision as the sign of the covenant. God promised that Sarah herself would bear a son, to be named Isaac, meaning "he laughs," a direct reference to Abraham's doubtful laughter at the news, given his and Sarah's ages. Abraham even suggested Ishmael could be the one to carry the promise instead, but God was clear: Isaac would be the son through whom the covenant continued, though Ishmael would be blessed as well.Sodom and GomorrahGod explained His purpose in choosing Abraham: so that he would lead his household to keep the way of the Lord through righteousness and justice. He then revealed His plan to destroy Sodom and Gomorrah for their sin, and Abraham pleaded with God on the cities' behalf, eventually landing on an agreement that God would spare them for the sake of just ten righteous people. When angels investigated, they found only four, Lot, his wife, and their two daughters. The angels' urgent instructions, get up, run, don't look back, don't stop, were framed as the same urgency we should feel toward sin in our own lives: get out of it, leave it behind, don't linger. The cities were destroyed, and as the family fled, Lot's wife looked back and was turned into a pillar of salt, a moment Jesus later referenced as a warning against longing for a world that's passing away instead of looking forward to what God has for us. None of this would have happened if Abraham had fully obeyed from the start and not brought Lot along in the first place. Abraham's imperfection showed up again later too, when he repeated the same lie about Sarah being his sister, nearly causing trouble with another king. What set him apart wasn't a lack of failure, but a consistent willingness to repent and return to obedience.The Ultimate TestSarah finally gave birth to Isaac when Abraham was 100 years old, just as promised. Later, once Isaac had grown, God tested Abraham in the hardest way possible, asking him to offer his son, his only son, the one he loved, as a sacrifice. This is the first mention of love in the entire Bible, tied to a father about to give up his son. Abraham didn't argue or complain. He obeyed, trusting that God would provide, even telling his son as much on the way up the mountain. The story carries an unmistakable echo of what God the Father would one day do with His own Son, carrying the wood for His own sacrifice, in full trust and obedience. Some Jewish historians place Isaac's age at the time around 33, the same age many believe Jesus was at the crucifixion.At the last moment, an angel stopped Abraham, telling him not to harm the boy, now knowing Abraham truly feared God since he hadn't withheld his only son. God's mercy prevailed, and because of Abraham's faithfulness, God reaffirmed His promise once more.A Pattern of Promise and TestingAcross the whole story, a pattern repeats: God calls and promises, Abraham is tested, and sometimes he fails, bringing Lot along, doubting through Ishmael, lying about Sarah, and sometimes he grows, interceding for Sodom, and ultimately offering Isaac in full surrender. God was patiently moving Abraham toward complete trust and obedience, and He succeeded. God's promises were never dependent on Abraham's perfection, only on God's own faithfulness, and that's exactly what makes Abraham's story an encouragement rather than an impossible standard.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.What promises did God make to Abram in Genesis 12, and how did they shape his journey?What is the significance of God changing Abram's and Sarai's names to Abraham and Sarah?In what ways do you see God's promises at work in your own life, even when you struggle with doubt or impatience?How can Abraham's journey of imperfect obedience encourage you when you feel like you've messed up or fallen short?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Has God ever asked you to wait on something, and how did you handle the waiting?Have you ever done something "mostly" obedient, kind of like Abraham bringing Lot along, and seen it cause problems later?What's something you're trusting God for right now that feels far off or uncertain?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuJune 28, 2026Redemption SeriesIdolatryLiam HungateAbout the SeriesThe Redemption Series follows the story of Scripture from Genesis to Revelation, tracing God's plan to save humanity. Tonight was the series' 20th lesson, and since a group of new freshmen joined for the first time, the night opened with a crash-course recap of everything covered so far before moving into tonight's passage.Genesis was summarized through eight "stepping stones," four pillars and four patriarchs:Creation: God made the heavens and the earth, including mankind, in six days.Fall: Adam and Eve's disobedience brought sin into the world and separated humanity from God.Flood: God wiped out a sinful world but preserved Noah and his family as a remnant.Tower: Sinful humanity tried to reach heaven by building the Tower of Babel, so God scattered them and confused their language.Abraham: The father of all believers, promised descendants as numerous as the stars.Isaac: Abraham's son, who carried the promise forward.Jacob: Renamed Israel, father of the twelve tribes.Joseph: Sold into slavery by his brothers, later used by God to save his family from famine.Exodus was summarized through four more:Moses: Raised in Pharaoh's household, called by God at the burning bush to free Israel from slavery.The Plagues: Ten judgments on Egypt after Pharaoh repeatedly refused to let Israel go.Passover: God struck down Egypt's firstborn but passed over homes marked with a lamb's blood, and Israel walked free.The Law: God gave Israel the Ten Commandments and more, showing them how to live as His people.The Tabernacle: A place where God's presence would dwell among His people.Passages: Exodus 32; Ezekiel 33:14-15What Was TaughtA Substitute for GodWith Moses gone forty days on the mountain, Israel grew impatient and asked Aaron to make them a god. They didn't reject God outright, they asked for a substitute, which is idolatry in its sneakiest form. Aaron, the same man who had worked closely with Moses and God, caved immediately, with no pushback and no prayer. Seeing miracles firsthand, the lesson pointed out, is not the same as being close to God.Aaron melted the people's gold jewelry into a calf, and Israel declared it the god who brought them out of Egypt, offering sacrifices to it. They were more excited about a statue that could do nothing for them than they had ever been about the God who had done everything for them, described as trading a winning lottery ticket for a scratch-off simply because the scratch-off was already in hand.Moses IntercedesOn the mountain, God told Moses what had happened, calling Israel "your people" rather than His own, and was ready to wipe the nation out and start over through Moses, the same way He had started over through Noah. Moses pleaded for Israel, not on the basis of anything they deserved, but by appealing to God's grace, His glory, and His goodness: they were the people God had already saved, destroying them would give Egypt reason to doubt Him, and He had made a promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. God relented, moving Israel from judgment to mercy.The point made here: God's warnings about sin are not cruelty, they're an invitation to turn back before the consequence lands, echoed in Ezekiel 33:14-15, where a person under judgment who turns from sin and does what is right will live. A coaching example was used alongside this: players are far more likely to memorize their team disciplines and verse when they know running is the consequence for not knowing them.The Broken TabletsAs Moses came down the mountain carrying the stone tablets God had written, he heard singing and saw Israel dancing around the golden calf. In anger, he broke the tablets, which the lesson framed as more than an emotional reaction. It was theological, a visible picture of the covenant Israel had already broken, similar to how a wedding ring handed back after infidelity didn't cause the broken vow but represents it.Moses tore down the calf, burned it, ground the remains into powder, mixed it into water, and made the Israelites drink it. When he confronted Aaron, Aaron blamed the people and claimed the calf had simply come out of the fire on its own. The lesson called this out plainly: Aaron took the path of least resistance because standing for God felt harder in the moment than going along with the crowd.Justice and MercyMoses called out, "Whoever is on the Lord's side, come to me," and only the Levites responded. Three thousand men died in the judgment that followed, and God later sent a plague on the rest of the people for what they had done. Grace was real here, but so was consequence. Mercy and justice were shown to coexist in God's character rather than cancel each other out.Moses Offers HimselfMoses went back up the mountain to intercede again, and this time offered to be blotted out in Israel's place. God told him no, because Moses was a sinner too and couldn't be the substitute. Moses stretched as far as a man could stretch and still fell short, which means whoever actually saves Israel, and us, has to be greater than Moses, greater than the Law, greater than the covenant. Hebrews points to Jesus as that greater high priest, the one who doesn't just intercede but gives Himself as the offering, and whose offering God accepts.Where This PointsThe lesson closed by naming three responses to a moment when God felt distant. Israel made a god they could control, one that asked nothing of them. Aaron took the path of least resistance, even though he knew better. Moses ran back toward God instead of away from Him. Students were asked which one describes them.Idols today were described the same way: not statues, but whatever we run to when things get hard and God feels quiet, a phone, a relationship, reputation, whatever numbs it. It rarely happens all at once. A hard week turns into an hour of scrolling instead of praying, then two hours, then it's the first thing reached for before even getting out of bed. Idols are appealing because they offer control with no waiting, no silence, and no faith required. The answer to God feeling distant was never to replace Him, but to do what Moses did: go back, pray hard, and hold onto who God is even when He can't be felt. And when that feels too hard, there is already a Savior who offered to take our place, and the Father said yes.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.Aaron took the path of least resistance because standing for God felt harder in the moment. When have you done the same thing, gone along with something because the pushback felt like too much?Our phones, relationships, and reputation aren't inherently bad things. So what's the line between something being good, and something being an idol?If you had been in that camp, if you were one of the people dancing around that calf, would you feel like you deserved Moses' offer of self-sacrifice? Why then do we treat what Jesus did like a fact we already know and take for granted? What should we do instead?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:What's something you reach for automatically when you're stressed or bored?Have you ever gone along with a group even though you knew better? What made it hard to speak up?What does "God feels distant" actually feel like for you, and what do you usually do when it happens?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuNovember 2, 2025Redemption SeriesPromise ContinuedLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight continued tracking God's promise through the Patriarchs, following the story forward from Abraham through his son Isaac and grandson Jacob. God had already promised to bless Abraham and, through his family line, the whole world. Tonight showed that same promise being carried forward, generation by generation, through some genuinely messy family history.Passages: Genesis 24-33, 49; Romans 9What Was TaughtGod's Promise Renewed Through IsaacAfter surviving the test on the altar, Isaac grew up, and God personally reaffirmed to him the same promise He'd made to Abraham: land, descendants as numerous as the stars, and blessing for the whole world through his line. Isaac married Rebekah.Two Nations in One WombRebekah became pregnant with twins, and the pregnancy was difficult enough that she sought God about it. He told her she was carrying two nations, that they would be divided, and that the older would serve the younger, a reversal of the expected order. The firstborn, Esau, meaning "hairy," was followed immediately by Jacob, whose name means "he grasps the heel," born holding onto his brother.A Birthright Traded, a Blessing StolenAs adults, Esau became a hunter while Jacob stayed close to home. One day, exhausted from the hunt, Esau traded away his birthright, the rights and inheritance due the firstborn son, for a bowl of Jacob's stew. Later, with his mother Rebekah's help, Jacob deceived his aging, blind father Isaac into giving him the blessing meant for Esau. When Esau returned and realized what had happened, both he and Isaac were devastated. Esau had now lost both his birthright and his blessing, exactly as God had foretold before either son was born. Enraged, Esau plotted to kill his brother, so Rebekah sent Jacob away to live with her brother Laban.Deception Comes Full CircleOn his journey, God appeared to Jacob and reaffirmed the same promise given to Abraham and Isaac. When Jacob arrived at Laban's home, he fell for Laban's daughter Rachel and agreed to work seven years to marry her. Laban, however, deceived Jacob into marrying his older daughter Leah first, requiring Jacob to work another seven years to also marry Rachel. Jacob loved Rachel more, which created deep tension in the household. God saw that Leah was unloved and gave her four sons, Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, while Rachel remained unable to conceive. In the rivalry that followed, both women gave their servants to Jacob to bear children on their behalf, echoing the earlier pattern of Sarah and Hagar, adding four more sons. Leah later had two more sons and a daughter. Finally, God opened Rachel's womb, and she gave birth to Joseph, whose name reflected both gratitude for what God had already done and hope for more to come.Wrestling With GodYears later, having grown wealthy, Jacob decided to return home, despite Esau's old threat still hanging over him. Learning that Esau was approaching with four hundred men, Jacob split his camp for safety and sent gifts ahead to try to soften his brother's anger. The night before their reunion, God Himself physically wrestled with Jacob and dislocated his hip, a lesson that what Jacob had spent his whole life fighting for, with his brother, with Laban, and now with God, could never be won through strength or manipulation, only through submission and dependence. God renamed him Israel, meaning "he struggles with God," and the limp that remained became a lifelong reminder that his strength was never his own.A Storybook ReunionThe next day, Esau ran to meet Jacob, embraced him, and the two brothers reconciled, a relationship restored in God's timing, not Jacob's own scheming.The Promise Passed DownLater in his life, Jacob passed the same promise and blessing down to his son Joseph. The promise didn't stop with Jacob. It carried through every generation that followed.Chosen by Grace, Not EffortRomans 9 explains why God carried His promise through Jacob rather than Esau. It wasn't favoritism. It was God being faithful to His own plan of redemption, a plan never based on human effort or birth order. Jacob didn't earn the promise, and Esau didn't lose it through any fault of his own. Paul makes the point directly: being a child of the promise, not simply physical descent, is what makes someone a true heir. The same grace that chose Jacob is what brings us into God's promise today, not through works, but through faith.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.How did Jacob end up receiving Isaac's blessing?What does Jacob's story teach us about trying to take control instead of trusting God's timing?God chose Jacob not because he earned it, but because of His grace. How does that truth change the way you see your relationship with God?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Have you ever tried to force something to happen your way instead of waiting on it?Is there a relationship in your life that needs the kind of reconciliation Jacob and Esau had?Do you ever feel like you have to earn God's favor? Where do you think that comes from?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuSeptember 23, 2026TopicalIt Is Okay To Not Be OkayAaron Capito About This MessageThis week was a standalone topical message on mental health. The goal was simple: help students see that God is not looking for people who have it all together. He is looking for honesty. Even the strongest people in the Bible had days they wanted to quit, and God's response was not disappointment. It was care.Aaron opened with a question: if you had to describe your week with an emoji, which one would it be, and which one would you actually post? The gap between those two answers is what the whole night was about.Passages: 1 Kings 18-19, Psalm 55:22, 2 Corinthians 12:8-10, Philippians 4:6-7What Was TaughtGrowing up in a "social media society"Students have grown up in a world where social media has become a competition to look put together: the best outfit, the best makeup, the latest sports win. Nothing posted is ever really casual. There is an unspoken rule about what is allowed. But nobody is perfect, and nobody is "normal." Everyone carries their own weight and troubles, and none of it shows up online.Mental health was defined as a state of mental and emotional well-being that lets people cope with life's stresses, realize their abilities, learn and work well, and contribute to their communities. The problem is that most of us know very little about it or how to handle it. So we copy the culture and pretend. We put on a fake face, even with the people who care about us.The Bible does not tell us to come to God looking okay. It tells us to come as we are. We come broken, and He makes us new and gives us joy.Elijah's mountaintop (1 Kings 18)Elijah had just had the biggest spiritual win of his life. He challenged the prophets of Baal: whichever God showed up would win. Baal's prophets cried out with no answer, and Elijah laughed at them. When Elijah called on the Lord, fire fell almost immediately and burned up the offering. Everyone saw God show up. That victory enraged Queen Jezebel.The crash (1 Kings 19:3-4)One threat from Jezebel, and Elijah ran for his life, sat under a tree, and asked God to let him die. "It is enough; now, O Lord." "I am no better than my fathers." This came right after his greatest victory, when you would expect him to be confident and fearless.The takeaway: there is nothing wrong with feeling defeated in scary moments. As Christians, we admit our shortcomings and know we are weak, and the threats of the world can get to us.Fear is not a sign that something is wrong with your faith.Uncertainty or worry does not mean you are doing something wrong.Aaron's storyAaron shared that near the end of his freshman year at Liberty, life was going great. On the night of the NFL Draft, his mom called. His brothers were coming to bring him home, he had to finish finals two weeks early, and he needed to leave within two days, because his dad was dying.He crashed just like Elijah. He ran to his room and wanted to be alone. He was honest that in those moments he doubted God. He could not see how God could meet him at the high and then throw him down low. But he did the only thing he knew to do in desperation: he called out to God. Four years later he still walks through low points after his dad's passing, and God is still leading him through the valley every day, keeping him dependent on Him.God's response: care, not anger (1 Kings 19:5-7)When Elijah cried out, God did not answer with anger or hurtful words. He sent an angel to comfort him and make sure he ate and rested, with a cake and water.Calling out to God did not make Aaron circumstances go away. His dad passed away. But God began to make sense of it and showed him how his story could be used in his ministry. God did not punish him for questioning or doubting. Psalm 55:22 tells us to cast our burden on the Lord, and He will sustain us. When we lay our burdens at His feet, He is not angry. He cares for us.We probably will not see angels bringing a meal to the house. But God sends people, Scripture, and opportunities. Friends, family, and church people came alongside our leader to make sure he felt loved, as the Spirit moved them to love him.The whisper (1 Kings 19:11-13)God did not show up in the wind, the earthquake, or the fire. He showed up in a gentle whisper.Many people treat God like a genie, or a "break in case of emergency" glass. They expect Him to show up big and loud, and only when something huge happens. But God is present in the small, personal spaces too. You will miss Him if you only look for a big move.After his dad died, Aaron kept asking for a big sign. He did not find God in the dramatic sign he was looking for. He found Him in the personal, intimate times: reading His Word, praying through tears, and being with other believers. God controls the big things, and He also takes close care of the small details of our lives. Sometimes He shows up quiet and close, and we miss it if we are only watching for something dramatic.Language for "not okay""Not okay" does not mean "not faithful." It means human.Naming it takes courage. Telling God or a trusted person how you feel is not weakness. It is the brave move, not the easy one.Stuffing it down makes it heavier. Bringing it to God or someone safe makes it shareable.Paul's thorn (2 Corinthians 12:8-10)Paul got personal in his letters. He wrote about a "thorn" that was tormenting him and asked God three times to take it away. God answered that His grace is sufficient and His power is made perfect in weakness. Paul's response was to boast in his weaknesses, because when he is weak, then he is strong.God uses our hardships to help us cling closer to Him, so our circumstances become opportunities to grow in faith. Paul only understood that by bringing it to God, and not once but three times. God meets us when we cry out, encourages us to do it, and uses what we go through to make us more like His Son.The challenge (Philippians 4:6-7)Philippians 4:6-7 does not say "don't feel anxious." It says bring it to God, specifically and out loud.Aaron was honest that there are still many days he is not okay. He still misses his dad, and some days that is hard. But four years in, he has learned he can bring his worries to God, and God meets him there, the same way He met Elijah in the whisper. And God has used his story the way He used Paul's thorn: to teach dependence and to be an example for others.It is okay to not be okay because we have access to the remedy: Christ and His completed work. Living in a fallen world, it is okay to be hurt, anxious, or scared. But it is not okay to sit in it. Bring your worries to God, and He will bring you through every trouble you face.Talk About It at HomeThese are the questions students talked through in small groups:Are you more likely to run to God in times of trouble, or when things are going great? In other words: in times of trouble, are you more likely to run to God or run away from Him?God didn't speak to Elijah through the wind, earthquake, or fire, but through a gentle whisper. What are some "quiet" ways God can remind us that He is with us?Example answers: the assurance of the Spirit, the beauty of creation, someone being inspired to reach out.Why can it be difficult to tell God or another person how we are really feeling?Example answers: "I'm scared of disappointment." "I don't want to burden them."What is one thing you can do this week when you're worried, stressed, or upset instead of keeping it all to yourself?Example answers: tell a friend, pray to God, read Scripture.A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:If you had to pick an emoji for your week, what would it be? Which one would you post?Do you think people online seem happier than they really are?When you're having a rough day, what actually helps?Is there anything I can be praying about for you this week?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuOctober 19, 2025Redemption SeriesJobLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight built on two prior weeks where Aaron taught on suffering, including the idea that suffering isn't from God but is allowed by Him and worked for our good, and the picture of a screw becoming stronger the more tightly it's fastened, the same way our faith grows stronger the more tightly we're fastened to Christ. Tonight put that theme into practice by walking through the entire book of Job.Passages: Job 1-42What Was TaughtA Righteous Man Loses EverythingJob lived during the time of the patriarchs and is described in Job 1:1 as a man of complete integrity who feared God and turned from evil. He was wealthy and devoted, so careful about his family's faithfulness that he offered sacrifices on his children's behalf just in case they had sinned unknowingly. Satan approached God and accused Job of only being faithful because his life was easy, arguing that if everything were taken away, Job would abandon his faith. God allowed the test, with the one condition that Satan couldn't physically harm Job. In rapid succession, Job lost his oxen and donkeys to raiders, his sheep and shepherds to fire, his camels to another raid, and finally all ten of his children, killed when a storm collapsed the house they were gathered in.Worship in the WreckageJob's response was to tear his robe and shave his head, public rituals of grief and stripped pride, and then fall down in worship. He said he came into the world with nothing and would leave with nothing, that everything he had belonged to God to begin with, and refused to curse God even in his devastation: "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away, blessed be the name of the Lord." When Satan afflicted him further with painful boils, Job's own wife told him to curse God and die. Job's answer: "Should we accept only good from God, and not adversity?" No trial turned him against God.Grief Without CursingNone of this means Job wasn't devastated. In chapter 3, he laments honestly, cursing the day he was born and wishing he'd never existed rather than face this level of suffering, grief God would address directly later in the book. This set up two questions the rest of the story wrestles with: does God's justice mean He simply rewards good behavior and punishes bad, and if good people suffer, does that mean God isn't just?Bad Theology From Good FriendsThree friends heard what happened and came to comfort Job, starting well by simply sitting with him in silence for a week. But they held a theology where obedience always brings reward and disobedience always brings punishment, so they concluded Job's suffering meant he must have sinned badly. Thirty chapters of arguing followed, with Job defending his innocence the whole way, until he grew tired of it and turned directly to God, demanding an explanation for what he was going through. A younger man named Elihu then entered angry, both at Job for justifying himself over God, and at the friends for being so quick to condemn him, insisting it's impossible for the ruler of the universe to be unjust.God Answers From the StormGod finally spoke to Job out of a storm in chapter 38, answering not with an explanation but with an overwhelming picture of His power and wisdom in creation. He pointed to Behemoth and Leviathan, two untamable creatures no human could ever control, to show Job that the world holds dangers and mysteries far beyond human strength or understanding, and that questioning God as though we grasp it all misses the point entirely.Restored, Not ExplainedJob's response, in chapter 42, was humility: he recognized God's wisdom and power far exceeded his own understanding, and chose to trust Him rather than demand answers. God then rebuked Job's friends for their false theology and restored Job, doubling his former wealth, gathering his extended family around him again, and blessing him with ten more children. Job lived another 140 years, saw four generations of his descendants, and died old and full of days.An Old Testament Picture of JesusJob's story reads like an early reflection of Christ: an innocent man treated as guilty, a target of Satan's attempts to pull him from God that ultimately failed and brought God more glory, suffering endured not as punishment but for a larger purpose, and trust in God's goodness held onto in the middle of real pain. Christ's death on the cross looked like defeat and became the doorway to His greatest victory. Job's story lands in the same place: God is greater than our suffering, and He remains just within it, even when His plan is beyond what we can fully understand.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.What false belief did Job's friends hold about suffering and sin?When you face loss or hardship, what is your first instinct, to question God or to worship Him like Job did?How does Job's example challenge your view of what it means to have faith in times of suffering?In what ways can you remind yourself that God is both good and just, even when His plan doesn't make sense?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:When something hard happens, do you tend to talk to God about it, or pull away from Him?Has anyone ever tried to explain your hard season to you in a way that felt wrong or unfair?What's something you don't understand about God or your circumstances right now that you're learning to trust Him with anyway?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuAugust 5, 2026The Gospel of JohnThe Betrayal and Arrest Part 1Aaron CapitoAbout the SeriesStudents are starting the beginning of the Crucifixion story, told through the Gospel of John. Aaron opened by asking students to imagine knowing the exact day they would die. Jesus lived with that reality. He knew not just that He would die, but when, and how brutally.The goal for this study is to see how Jesus faced that reality: with confidence and clarity, not panic. Part one covers His betrayal by Judas, His arrest, and the first of Peter's denials.Passages: John 18:1-18What Was TaughtJesus knew what was coming, and went anywayJesus led His disciples to a garden that Judas, His betrayer, already knew well. Aaron pointed out that Jesus wasn't hiding. He went to a place He knew Judas could find Him, because Jesus knew His mission and knew the cost of it: His death was the only way humanity could be saved.When soldiers arrived to arrest Him, Jesus asked who they were looking for, already knowing the answer, and stepped forward instead of running. Aaron's challenge to students: where is God calling you to be on mission, and are you being obedient to that call even when it's uncomfortable? It's okay to feel scared. Jesus likely did too. But He didn't quit when obedience got hard, and neither should we.Jesus stayed in control, even in chainsWhen Jesus said "I am he," the soldiers arresting Him fell backward, apparently thrown off by His calm. Jesus then asked that His disciples be let go, a moment John ties back to Jesus's earlier promise that He would lose none of those the Father gave Him. Even at His own arrest, Jesus was protecting His people.Aaron drew out the bigger point: God's followers aren't promised long or comfortable lives, but they are protected for God's purposes until He calls them home. If God still has work for you to do, nothing can stop you. When that work is finished, nothing can keep you here either. Death, for a believer, isn't a loss. It's being called home.Peter tried to help. Jesus didn't need it.When Peter drew a sword and struck a servant's ear, Jesus told him to put it away, asking, "shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?" That phrase, "the cup," echoes Jesus's own prayer in the garden of Gethsemane, where He asked the Father if there was another way, then submitted to His will anyway.Aaron compared Peter to a time he ignored his GPS because he was sure he knew a faster route, then hit construction and was late for work. Peter thought he understood the situation better than Jesus did. He didn't. Aaron asked students where in their own lives they might be trying to avoid or fix something God has actually placed them in.Jesus was then brought before Annas, a former high priest still pulling strings behind the scenes, before being sent to Caiaphas, the current high priest. Aaron compared Annas to a retired coach the new coach still keeps around for advice. The religious leaders thought they finally had control over Jesus. John's point is that they never did. Jesus was in chains, and still in control of the story.Peter denied HimPeter followed Jesus into the high priest's courtyard, and when a servant girl asked if he was one of Jesus's disciples, Peter said no. It's the first of three denials Peter will make before a rooster crows, just as Jesus predicted.Aaron drew two points from this. First, Jesus was completely alone. Even His closest disciple abandoned Him. Second, fear can push faithful believers into compromise. Aaron compared it to wearing your favorite team's jersey into a room full of rival fans and quietly zipping up your hoodie. You don't stop being a fan. You just don't want anyone to know. Peter still loved Jesus. He just didn't want anyone to know it in that moment, because it had become dangerous.Aaron's challenge: the biggest threat to our faith usually isn't people who hate Jesus. It's our own fear of what people will think of us for following Him. Christians are called to be unashamed, echoing Paul's words in Romans that he was not ashamed of the gospel because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.Aaron closed by restating the gospel plainly: humanity is sinful and deserving of death, but God sent His Son to live a sinless life and take our punishment anyway, so that we could be reconciled, or restored to a right relationship, with God.Talk About It at HomeThese are the questions the group discussed:Jesus knew He was walking towards suffering. Why didn't he run away?What's something God calls Christians to do that feels scary? Why?When have you felt pressure to hide your faith so you'd fit in?What's one practical way you can be unashamed of Jesus this week?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:If you knew you only had a limited amount of time left, what would you want to do differently?Has a friend or teammate ever let you down when you needed them? What was that like?Is there a time you went along with the crowd instead of saying what you actually believed?Who's someone you know who isn't afraid to talk about their faith? What's that like to watch?‍

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuMay 3, 2026Redemption SeriesMannaLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight returned to the book of Exodus, picking up with Israel shortly after they'd left the oasis of Elim and continued their journey toward Mount Sinai. It had only been about a month since they crossed the Red Sea and left Egypt, but tonight showed what happens when God's provision meets a people who forget how much they've already been given.The lesson opened with the true story of the Berlin Airlift. When the Soviets cut off every road, train, and canal into West Berlin in 1948, leaving two million people with about a month of food left, the Allies began flying supplies in around the clock for nearly a year. One pilot, Gail Halvorsen, started dropping candy to children at the fence on little parachutes, and other pilots joined him. Those kids couldn't earn the help or reach it themselves. All they could do was look up and trust the planes would keep coming. That's the picture for tonight.Passages: Exodus 16-17; John 6What Was TaughtBread from Heaven, and a Lesson in TrustA month into the wilderness, Israel was already complaining to Moses and Aaron, saying they'd rather have stayed enslaved in Egypt than face hunger in the desert. They weren't starving, just uncomfortable, and their complaints conveniently forgot that they'd been crying out to God for rescue back in captivity. God responded anyway, sending bread from heaven, manna, with a daily portion for every family.There were rules built in to test their obedience: collect only enough for one day, except on the sixth day, when they could collect a double portion to rest on the seventh. Leftover manna spoiled overnight and filled with worms, except on the sixth day, when it stayed good through the Sabbath. This was Israel's first real introduction to the Sabbath, a day of rest built into how God provided for them. God could have met their complaining with discipline. Instead He blessed them with both manna and quail, teaching them ongoing dependence on Him. Moses later had a day's portion preserved as a testimony for future generations, and Israel would eat manna for the next forty years, until they reached the edge of Canaan.Why the Wilderness Took So LongIsrael wandered forty years before reaching the Promised Land, even though God Himself was guiding them the whole time by cloud and fire. He deliberately led them the long way around to avoid threats on the main route, and used the time to grow their faith, obedience, and dependence on Him. It also became a season of pruning: many in that generation were unfaithful, and God used the years in the wilderness to prepare their children, the generation that would actually enter the land knowing Him.Water from the Rock and a Battle Won in PrayerIn Exodus 17, Israel complained again, this time about water, until Moses cried out to God for help. God sent him ahead with his staff to Mount Horeb, where He provided water out of a rock in front of the people.Soon after, the Amalekites launched a surprise attack, Israel's first experience of battle. Moses sent Joshua to lead the fighting while he, Aaron, and Hur climbed a nearby hill. As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel had the advantage in battle, but the effort wore on him, so Aaron and Hur held his arms up until the battle was won. Moses wasn't just holding up his hands. He was interceding in prayer for Israel and for Joshua, and the outcome of that battle rested on those prayers being sustained.I Will ProvideBy this point Israel had seen manna fall from heaven, quail sent for food, water drawn from a rock, and a battle won through prayer. The pattern was clear: God provides. But it's easy to focus on the physical ways God provides and miss the ultimate provision behind all of it.The Bread That Doesn't Run OutFast forward about 1,400 years to John 6, where Jesus had just fed five thousand people with five loaves of bread. The crowd wanted to crown Him king on the spot, so He withdrew, and the next day they chased Him down again, wanting another sign like the manna Moses gave their ancestors. Jesus corrected them: Moses didn't give their ancestors that bread, God did, and now Jesus Himself is the true bread from heaven.The picture running through the whole night had been of a God who watches over His people and sends exactly what they need from above. Here, Jesus flips it: He isn't only the one sending the provision, He is the provision. That didn't sit well with the crowd, who started grumbling, just like the Israelites once did in the wilderness. Jesus pressed further: manna kept Israel alive for a day, but even after forty years of it, that whole generation still died. He offers something manna never could, bread that sustains forever. Provision was never the same thing as salvation. Manna can't save. Jesus can.Some Walked Away, One StayedThis teaching was hard to hear, hard enough that many of Jesus' own disciples, people who had eaten the bread, watched the miracles, and heard Him teach, turned back and stopped following Him. Jesus turned to the Twelve and asked if they wanted to leave too. Peter's answer: where else would they go? Jesus has the words of eternal life. The question left hanging in the room: which one are you, the ones who walked away, or the one who stayed?Receiving the BreadThe night closed with a picture of how to receive Jesus, the same way Israel received the manna: aware of the need, hungry and ready to receive it, enough for ourselves and our families, done daily, approached with humility, and received with gratitude, knowing it isn't deserved. Not just admired from a distance, but taken in and made part of who we are.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.Jesus had just fed 5,000 people, healed the sick, and walked on water. By the end of John 6, many of His disciples walk away from Him. What does that tell you about the difference between being impressed by Jesus and actually following Him? Which one describes most of your week?Jesus said, "your fathers ate the manna and they died," meaning even God's provision isn't the same as God Himself. What are the "manna" things in your life right now, God's good gifts, that you might be mistaking for Jesus Himself? Be specific.Jesus asked the Twelve straight up, "Do you want to go away as well?" If He asked you that today, not at a retreat, not at camp, but on a regular Tuesday, what would your honest answer be? What does that answer reveal about where you actually are with Him?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Have you ever complained about something good because you were focused on what you didn't have?Who's someone who kept showing up for you even when you didn't fully appreciate it at the time?What's something you enjoy about faith or church that might actually be a stand-in for a real relationship with Jesus?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuAugust 26, 2026The Gospel of JohnThe Crucifixion Part 1Aaron CapitoAbout the SeriesThis week's message looked at John 19:1-16, the first part of a two part study on the Crucifixion. It covers Jesus' flogging, His trial in front of Pilate, and Pilate finally handing Him over to be crucified.Passages: John 19:1-16What Was TaughtWhy the Bigger Picture MattersThe message opened with a recent UFC title fight. To someone without any background on the sport, a photo of the two fighters afterward would make it look like the wrong man won: one fighter looked barely touched, the other looked beaten up. But anyone who knew the full fight understood the beaten up fighter had actually dominated. Having the full picture changes how you read what you're looking at.That's the lens for John 19. Jesus' beating and mocking before the cross can look like a loss. But knowing who He is and what He was accomplishing shows the opposite: He wasn't losing. He was winning, decisively.The Flogging and Mockery (John 19:1-3)Pilate had Jesus flogged: struck repeatedly with a multi strand leather whip, sometimes fitted with pieces of bone or metal, designed to cause serious injury, not just pain. Soldiers forced a crown of thorns onto His head and dressed Him in a purple robe, then mocked Him as "King of the Jews" while striking Him with their hands.The point: Jesus, as God, could have stopped it at any moment. Like someone tapping out of a chokehold to signal they've had enough, Jesus could have tapped out of suffering He didn't deserve. He chose to endure it instead.Behold the Man (John 19:4-9)Pilate brought the beaten Jesus out, still wearing the crown and robe, to show the crowd he found no guilt in Him. The chief priests and officers still demanded He be crucified. The Jewish leaders pointed to their law: claiming to be the Son of God was, in their eyes, blasphemy worthy of death (see Leviticus 24:16).But Jesus never blasphemed. He lived a perfect life, performed miracles people saw with their own eyes, and quoted Scripture with total understanding. When Pilate heard the claim that Jesus said He was God's Son, John says he became even more afraid. Even a man who didn't believe was shaken by the possibility that it was true.The takeaway: how you see Jesus determines how you respond to Him. If He's just a good teacher, you can shrug Him off. If He's the Son of God, He's not someone you simply listen to. He's someone you surrender to.Authority From Above (John 19:9-11)Pilate asked Jesus where He was from, and Jesus stayed silent, which confused and angered Pilate. He reminded Jesus he had the authority to either release Him or crucify Him: the choice was his. Jesus answered that Pilate's authority only existed because it had been given to him from above.The point: God is sovereign even over the actions of sinful people. Jesus' beating and the crucifixion ahead of Him were genuinely evil acts committed by sinful people, and yet God used them to accomplish the greatest good imaginable: the salvation of sinners. When we go through suffering or situations we don't understand, we can trust God hasn't lost control, even when we can't see what He's doing.We Have No King but Caesar (John 19:12-16)The Jewish leaders pressured Pilate by threatening his loyalty to Caesar: releasing someone who claimed to be a king would make Pilate look disloyal to Rome. Pilate presented Jesus one more time, saying, "Behold your King!" The leaders answered, "We have no king but Caesar," even though they claimed to follow God. That's the irony of these verses: people who said they served the Lord chose an earthly ruler over Him, then demanded the death of the very God they claimed to serve. Pilate handed Jesus over to be crucified.The message pointed out that it wasn't only the anger of that crowd that put Jesus on the cross. It was our sin too, and it's His finished work that gives us life.Main point of the message: Jesus endured what He did not deserve so that we could receive what we could never earn. He wasn't a helpless victim. He was the King who endured, the Son of God who willingly suffered, the innocent man who took the place of the guilty, because of His love for us.Talk About It at HomeUse these to keep the conversation going after service:Jesus could have stopped His suffering at any moment, but He chose to endure it. Why do you think Jesus was willing to suffer for us even though He didn't deserve any of it? Follow-up: What does that teach us about how much Jesus loves us?John 19 shows us that different people saw Jesus in very different ways. Pilate saw an innocent man. The Jewish leaders saw someone they wanted to kill. But Jesus really was the Son of God. Why does it matter that we recognize Jesus for who He really is? Follow-up: What are some ways people today might view Jesus incorrectly?Jesus told Pilate that he would have no authority over Him unless it had been given "from above." How can knowing that God is still in control help us when we're going through something difficult that we don't understand?The Jewish leaders said, "We have no king but Caesar," even though they claimed to follow God. What are some things that can become more important to us than following Jesus? Follow-up: How can we recognize when something is starting to take Jesus' place in our lives?Our main point was: "Jesus endured what He did not deserve so that we could receive what we could never earn." What does that mean to you personally? How should knowing that Jesus died for your sins change the way you live?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:What's one hard thing you did even though you didn't want to, because it would help someone else?Have you ever had to trust someone even when you didn't understand what they were doing? What was that like?Why do you think it matters what we actually believe about Jesus, not just what we've heard about Him?What's one way you could show love to someone this week, even if it's hard?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuJuly 27, 2025Redemption SeriesThe FallLiam HungateAbout the SeriesAfter two weeks on Creation, including Jesus' presence and role in it, tonight moved into Genesis 3 and the Fall of man.Passages: Genesis 3What Was TaughtSatan's Origin and Opening MoveThe serpent in the garden is Satan, and the lesson gave some background on him: Ezekiel 28 describes him as one of the highest-ranking angels, a leader of worship in heaven, and Isaiah 14 attributes his fall to jealousy and a desire to be equal to or greater than God. Ever since, he's worked to pull people away from God, something only overcome through Jesus.His opening move with Eve was a question: "Did God really say...?" The lesson called this Satan's ongoing strategy, planting doubt about what God has actually said, with modern examples like "did God really say not to get drunk," "did God really say to save yourself for marriage," "did He really say marriage is between a man and a woman," and "did He really say Jesus is the only way to heaven." It was compared to clickbait: technically containing a half-truth, but designed to mislead.The Serpent's LieEve's response to the serpent added a detail God hadn't actually said, that touching the fruit would also bring death, suggesting she'd only heard the command secondhand. The serpent flatly denied any consequence would follow, then escalated: eating the fruit would make her like God, knowing good and evil. That's the same temptation that led to Satan's own fall, and here he used it to paint sin as desirable and God as petty and withholding.Whose Fault Was It, Really?Eve ate the fruit and gave some to Adam, who the text says was with her the whole time. The lesson pushed back on any instinct to place the blame solely on Eve: Adam was the one who received God's command directly, was physically present, and did nothing to stop it. That failure to act was named the "sin of omission," distinct from Eve's "sin of commission," using the illustration of someone standing by and watching everyone else clean up a room instead of pitching in themselves, not wrong in the active sense, but still a failure to do right. In that light, Adam's failure to lead and protect his wife was framed as the true original sin, more than Eve's act itself, since Eve had been deceived while Adam disobeyed with full knowledge.This connected to a brief note on the one unforgivable sin, blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, explained not as a specific bad act but as an ongoing refusal to receive the forgiveness God offers, itself a kind of sin of omission.Hiding From GodOnce they ate, shame entered the picture immediately, and they covered themselves and hid. The lesson explained God's appearance walking in the garden as a Christophany, a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ, since no one has ever seen God the Father directly. When God called out, "Where are you?", it wasn't posed as an interrogation from someone who didn't already know the answer, but as the grief of a father who now sensed distance between himself and his children because of their sin.Blame and DenialAdam's response was to blame Eve, and indirectly God Himself, for giving him "the woman." Eve, in turn, blamed the serpent. The lesson connected this directly to a pattern that hasn't gone away: avoiding guilt and shame by pointing the finger elsewhere instead of owning what we've done.A Curse and a PromiseGod cursed the serpent to crawl and "eat dust" in defeat, and declared lasting hostility between it and humanity.
