Genesis 3:15, "he will strike your head, and you will strike his heel," was explained as the earliest prophecy of the gospel: the Messiah would be wounded by Satan but would ultimately deal him a fatal blow. Even in the middle of pronouncing judgment, God was already announcing His plan to redeem what had just been broken. His purpose was never simply innocent people in a garden, it was always redeemed people.The Curse on Man and WomanThe woman's curse included pain in childbirth and a struggle within marriage for control. The man's curse included painful labor, a ground that would now produce thorns and thistles, and mortality, returning to the dust he was made from.Clothed by GraceAdam named his wife Eve, "mother of all the living," a name that carried the promise of the coming seed who would ultimately defeat Satan. God then made clothing from animal skins for them, requiring a sacrifice, since there's no atonement without the shedding of blood. Even within moments of their fall, God was already providing for them, covering their shame with a garment paid for by another life, a preview of how believers are later clothed in righteousness through the life of Jesus.Mercy in ExileGod sent Adam and Eve out of Eden and guarded the way back to the tree of life. What can look purely like punishment was actually mercy: sparing them from living forever in a sinful, fallen state. Scripture doesn't say what became of the garden after this, though it's reasonable to assume it was left to the effects of the curse over time.Every Curse, Reversed in ChristThe lesson closed by walking through each piece of the curse and how Christ directly answered it: sin brought pain to childbirth, and Christ brought glory through His own suffering; sin brought conflict, and Christ endured conflict to secure our salvation; the curse brought thorns, and Christ wore a crown of them; sin brought sweat and toil, and Christ sweat drops of blood in His own struggle; sin brought sorrow, and Christ became a man well acquainted with grief to save us; sin brought death, and Christ tasted death for everyone so we wouldn't have to face it alone.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.What was the first question the serpent asked Eve, and why was it significant?What is the difference between the sin of commission and the sin of omission? Which did Adam and Eve commit?Why do you think Satan's main strategy is to get us to doubt God's Word? How do you see this happening in your own life or in the world today?If God's plan was always to redeem us, even after the Fall, how should that change the way you approach Him when you mess up?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Have you ever heard something that sounded almost true, but was actually twisted just enough to mislead you?When something goes wrong, is your first instinct to own it or to point somewhere else?What's a "curse" or hard season in your life where you can see God already at work redeeming it?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuMarch 15, 2026Redemption SeriesMosesLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight moved the Redemption Series out of Genesis and into the book of Exodus, picking up right where Joseph left off: settled in Egypt with his father Jacob and the rest of the family. Genesis had been mapped out through eight "stepping stones," Creation, Fall, Flood, Tower, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. The next stepping stone into Exodus is the man at the center of tonight's lesson: Moses.Passages: Exodus 1-2; Hebrews 11:23-26What Was TaughtA Forgotten PeopleSeventy Israelites moved to Egypt under Joseph's protection, and over roughly 400 years, their descendants multiplied rapidly. As generations passed, Joseph was forgotten, and with him went the favor his memory had provided. A new king rose who didn't know Joseph and feared Israel's growing numbers, worried they might side with a rival group against Egypt. He responded with forced labor as a calculated way to control them. The lesson drew a direct line here to patterns seen throughout history in antisemitism, fear of a growing population, followed by dehumanizing and blaming that group. None of it worked. Israel kept multiplying, because God's promise to Abraham couldn't be stopped by affliction.Choosing God Over PharaohWhen forced labor failed to slow Israel's growth, Pharaoh escalated to attempted genocide, ordering Hebrew midwives to kill every baby boy at birth. The midwives refused, fearing God more than the king, and God blessed them with families of their own. Israel kept growing anyway. The point made here: when a government's command conflicts with God's will, God comes first. Pharaoh's next move was even broader, ordering every Israelite boy thrown into the Nile.Drawn Out of the WaterMoses was born into this danger, a descendant of Levi. His mother hid him for three months, then, unable to hide him any longer, placed him in a waterproofed basket among the reeds of the Nile. Pharaoh's own daughter found him and, moved by compassion, defied her father's decree to save him. Moses' sister, watching nearby, arranged for the baby's own mother to nurse and raise him in his early years, even being paid for it. Pharaoh's daughter later formally adopted him and named him Moses, meaning "drawn out," bringing him into the royal family with access to Egypt's finest education and privilege.Even surrounded by that privilege, Moses' heritage and his mother's early influence kept him rooted in faith. Hebrews 11 commends exactly that: by faith his parents hid him without fear of the king's decree, and by faith Moses later refused the title of Pharaoh's daughter's son, choosing to suffer alongside God's people rather than enjoy Egypt's fleeting pleasures, valuing the reproach of Christ above all of Egypt's treasure.Rejected, Then HumbledAround age 40, moved by sympathy for his people, Moses killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew slave. The next day, trying to mediate a dispute between two Hebrews, he was rejected and scolded instead, a moment the lesson compared to Jesus being initially rejected in His own right to be prince and judge over Israel. When Pharaoh learned what Moses had done, Moses fled for his life to Midian.Learning to Be NobodyIn Midian, Moses helped a priest named Reuel's daughters water their flock. Invited to dinner as thanks, he was given a place to stay and Reuel's daughter Zipporah in marriage. They had a son, Gershom, meaning "stranger," a name that captured Moses' sense of belonging fully to neither Egypt nor Israel. The shift was described plainly: in Egypt, Moses learned how to be somebody. In Midian, he learned how to be nobody, exactly the kind of humbling God used to prepare him for what came next.God Was Never SilentPharaoh eventually died, but Israel remained enslaved and cried out to God. Exodus closes this section with God hearing their cry and remembering His covenant. Though God seemed silent through these two chapters, He was working behind the scenes the whole time, the same way He still works during our own seasons of waiting. No empire, government, or uprising can stop what God has promised, and there's an invitation in that to see ourselves the same way: used by Him, kept within His promises, and willing to be used.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.What are some ways a culture can "forget" what God has done in the past? What does that look like today?Why do you think the midwives chose to obey God even though it could have cost them their lives? What are some times today when Christians have to choose between obeying authority versus God?Why do you think God sometimes works quietly or behind the scenes rather than in obvious ways? Have you ever looked back and noticed God's quiet hand in your life?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Has there ever been a season where it felt like God was quiet? What happened when you looked back on it later?Have you ever had to choose between what someone in authority told you to do and what you knew was right?What's a time you felt "humbled" that ended up teaching you something important?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuAugust 10, 2025Redemption SeriesThe Fall: Part 2Liam HungateAbout the SeriesTwo weeks ago, the group covered the Fall in Genesis 3: Satan's temptation, Adam and Eve's disobedience, and the promise of redemption tucked inside the curse God gave the serpent. Tonight continued into Genesis 4 and the story of their sons, Cain and Abel.Passages: Genesis 4; Psalm 51What Was TaughtGod's Design for IntimacyGenesis 4 opens with the Bible's first mention of intimacy between a husband and wife, Adam and Eve. The Hebrew word used there means "to know," pointing to a closeness that comes specifically from the covenantal bond of marriage, not from physical intimacy on its own. The lesson contrasted that with today's cultural message to "try it out" with someone before committing, naming it directly as a reversal of God's actual design. Heading back into a school environment full of that same cultural pressure, students were encouraged to hold onto God's design regardless, while also being reminded that it's never too late to turn back to it, even after failure, pointing to Jonah, David, and Paul as examples. The challenge left with them: be a light in that environment, not blend into it.A Misplaced HopeEve named her first son Cain, meaning roughly "I've got him" or "here he is," likely believing he was the promised offspring who would defeat the serpent from Genesis 3. That hope would turn out to be badly misplaced.Two Brothers, Two OfferingsAbel became a shepherd, a role that echoes Christ as shepherd of His people, while Cain worked the cursed ground. When the time came to bring an offering to God, Abel gave the firstborn and best portions of his flock, while Cain brought only some of his produce. God regarded Abel's offering and not Cain's, and Hebrews 11:4 explains why: Abel offered his in faith. Cain's offering, by contrast, looked more like empty religious motion than real worship, reflected in the noticeably lesser quality of what he brought.Jealousy Takes RootCain responded with anger and despair at being rejected, rooted in wounded pride that his younger brother had been accepted by God and he hadn't. The lesson pushed back gently on any instinct to feel distant from this story: sibling arguments that carry real hatred aren't so different, and Scripture treats hatred itself as murder already committed in the heart.A Loving Warning, IgnoredGod spoke directly to Cain, telling him he could still be accepted if he did what was right, warning that sin was crouching at the door wanting to control him, but that he could and must rule over it instead. The point made here: we either end up mastered by sin, or mastered by Christ, and ruling over sin starts with letting God rule over us first.The First MurderDespite that warning, Cain lured Abel out to a field and killed him, the first death and the first murder in Scripture, carried out deliberately rather than in a sudden fit of rage. The son once hoped to be humanity's promised redeemer instead became its first murderer. Abel's name, fittingly, means "breath" or "vapor," a life that vanished as quickly as it began.A Chance to Confess, a Lie InsteadWhen God asked Cain where his brother was, it was an open door to confess. Cain lied instead, answering with the now-famous line, "Am I my brother's keeper?", ironic given that as the older brother, protecting Abel was exactly his role. The lesson compared this kind of senseless jealousy-driven violence to two coworkers turning on each other simply over who gets more attention or credit, as absurd as that sounds out loud. Jude 1:11 later warns believers against "the way of Cain," a pattern of greed and jealousy that never really went away.Cursed and Cast OutGod's judgment on Cain, the third curse recorded in the Bible, went further than the one given to Adam: where Adam would struggle to work the ground, Cain would find it wouldn't yield to him at all, and where Adam lost his home in Eden, Cain would become a restless wanderer with no home anywhere. Cain's response wasn't repentance, only a complaint that the punishment was too severe, a reaction the lesson tied to how often people today respond to consequences with "that's not fair" instead of owning what they did. Even so, God showed Cain mercy, placing a protective mark on him so no one would kill him, a reminder that God values human life even in someone actively rejecting Him.From Guilt to GraceOn the surface, this story seems to have nothing redemptive in it: parents who introduced sin to the world, one son dead, the other a murderer and an outcast. When guilt and regret run that deep, the lesson pointed to Psalm 51, David's prayer after his affair with Bathsheba and his role in her husband's death, written once the prophet Nathan confronted him. The contrast drawn was direct: where Cain reacted to being confronted with denial and self-pity, David responded with genuine repentance.Seth and the Promised LineGenesis 4 closes with the birth of a third son, Seth, meaning "appointed" or "placed." With Cain's line cursed and Abel's cut short, Seth became the one through whom the promised line, eventually leading to Christ, would continue. Nothing about this family's failure derailed God's plan. The closing picture was bowling with the bumpers up: when we drift off course, God's grace works like those bumpers, redirecting us back rather than letting us land in the gutter. Even here, redemption was already at work.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.According to Hebrews 11:4, what made Abel's offering "better" than Cain's?Have you ever felt jealous or angry like Cain? How did you respond, and what could you have done differently?How can you "rule over" sin in your own life, as God encouraged Cain to do?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Has jealousy of someone close to you ever gotten out of hand? What happened?When you mess up, is your first instinct to make excuses or to own it?What does it look like for you to be a "light" in a place where the culture pulls the other way?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuApril 19, 2026Redemption SeriesPlaguesLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight stepped back in the Redemption Series to look at what it took to get to the moment covered last week, when Moses led Israel out of Egypt and through the Red Sea. Before that could happen, God had to press Pharaoh through a series of ten plagues.The night opened with a picture of ignoring a smoke alarm at night, not just once, but pulling the battery every single time it goes off, for ten nights straight. Eventually the house burns down. That's exactly what Pharaoh did with ten unmistakable warnings from God.Passages: Exodus 4-11What Was TaughtGod Qualifies the CalledBack at the burning bush, God gave Moses three signs to prove he'd been sent: his shepherd's staff became a snake and then a staff again, his hand turned leprous and then was healed, and a third sign involving water. Even after seeing this, Moses doubted he was capable of speaking for God. God's answer was direct: He made Moses' mouth, and He would be with it. God doesn't just call the qualified, He qualifies the called. Moses still resisted, so God grew angry but still provided a solution, sending Aaron along as the spokesman while Moses led.A Hardening HeartAs Moses and Aaron headed back to Egypt, God told Moses plainly that Pharaoh's firstborn would eventually pay the price for holding God's firstborn, Israel, captive. Pharaoh's heart hardening became the theme to track through the whole night, compared to a callus: the first blow hurts, but after enough repetition, the skin stops feeling it at all.Israel believed Moses and Aaron right away, but Pharaoh flatly refused God's request and made Israel's labor even harder in response. Yet God reaffirmed His covenant with a string of promises: I will bring you out, I will rescue you, I will redeem you, I will take you as my people, I will be your God, I will bring you into the land, I will give it to you as your own. All that was asked of Israel was trust.Ten Plagues, One PatternThe first plague turned Egypt's water to blood. Egyptian magicians copied the trick through demonic power, which only hardened Pharaoh further, but they could never reverse what they imitated, the same way counterfeit money can look real without ever holding real value. From there, the plagues escalated: frogs Pharaoh begged to have removed, then refused to release Israel once relief came; gnats, which the magicians couldn't replicate at all; flies, with God drawing a clear line between Egypt and His own people; the death of Egyptian livestock while Israel's flocks were spared; and painful boils breaking out on people and animals alike, described like the worst kind of sunburn blister covering the whole body.It's during the boils, in Exodus 9:12, that the text first says the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart. The point made here: God wasn't acting against Pharaoh, He was affirming the choice Pharaoh had already made over and over. The plagues continued with the worst hailstorm Egypt had ever seen, locusts stripping the land bare, and finally three days of total darkness, so complete that no one could see or move, except in the areas where Israel lived. Only the tenth and final plague, Passover and the death of the firstborn, remained, already covered the week before.Every Plague, a Dismantled GodEach of the ten plagues directly exposed a specific Egyptian god as powerless. The Nile, worshipped as a source of life, became death. The frog-headed goddess of fertility was buried under an unclean swarm of frogs. Geb, god of the earth, couldn't stop dust from becoming gnats. Egypt's god of insects couldn't control the flies. The sacred bull and cow goddess couldn't protect their own livestock. The magicians tied to Egypt's gods of healing couldn't stand against the boils. The gods of sky and storm were absent when hail fell. Osiris, god of agriculture, couldn't save the crops from locusts. Ra, the sun god, Egypt's most important deity and the one Pharaoh himself claimed descent from, couldn't turn the light back on. And the final plague struck Pharaoh directly, the one Egypt worshipped as untouchable, through the death of his own son.One layer at a time, God dismantled everything Egypt trusted: their environment, their health, their leadership, their religion, like pulling blocks from a tower until it finally falls.Responding or ResistingGod reveals His power to show us who He is, but our response to that revelation determines what it means for us. Israel and Moses responded in faith and were rescued. Pharaoh resisted again and again and was met with judgment. Same God, different outcomes, depending on the response. God still reveals Himself today, through circumstances, through people, and through His Word, and people still resist Him just as Pharaoh did. Hearts are always doing one of two things: softening or hardening.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.What are some idols today that people put their trust in instead of God? Why is it so easy to trust in stuff we can see instead of Him?If God wanted your full attention, what do you think He'd take away first?Have you ever ignored something that you knew was the right thing? What happened?Are you more like Israel or Pharaoh right now, and why? What's the difference between hearing God and listening to Him?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Have you ever ignored a warning sign, big or small, and regretted it later?What's something you trust or rely on that could let you down if you're not careful?Do you feel like your heart is more soft or more hardened toward God lately?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuAugust 19, 2026TopicalSpiritual Blessing in Christ: Who Am I? Aaron CapitoThis week's focus: who you are in Christ, not who the world says you are.Students often define themselves by things that can change: friends, grades, interests, even how they feel about themselves. This week's message asked them to set those aside and ask a harder question: does who I think I am line up with who God says I am?Passages: Ephesians 1:3-14What Was TaughtChosen before the world beganPaul opens Ephesians by blessing God for the blessings He has given us in Christ. Before he tells Christians what to do, he tells them who they are. Paul says God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, meaning before creation itself, God already had a purpose for His people.To picture the size of that love, Aaron shared about his own dad, who worked full time in the military while his mom stayed home. Money was tight, but his dad quietly set some aside so the family could take vacations. His dad's sacrifice, made out of love, was a small picture of what God does for us on a far bigger scale. If we understand how much God has invested in us, we should give everything back to Him.Adopted into God's familyPaul says God predestined us for adoption, meaning He determined in advance, before the world began, that we would be brought into His family through Jesus. He didn't just think of us ahead of time. He saved us, and He did it for a reason: to be His hands and feet in the world. We weren't just saved to spend eternity with God. We were saved to serve Him now.Aaron illustrated this with a line from Hulk in Avengers Endgame: "It's like I was made for this." Realizing we were made for more than just living, but for serving God, changes how we walk and talk day to day.This adoption is possible only because of what Christ finished on the cross. Grace, meaning receiving something we don't deserve, is what makes all of it possible. God was willing to die for us. That is how much our identity matters to Him.Redeemed and forgivenThrough Christ's blood we have redemption, which means being bought back or set free at a cost, and forgiveness of our sins. Paul says God lavished, or generously poured out, His grace on us. Christ's death for us wasn't an obligation He grudgingly carried out. It came from love and compassion.Paul also says God made known to us the mystery of His will: how everything will ultimately be united in Christ. That matters because we live in a broken world full of fear and anxiety about what's next. Christians can rest knowing Christ has already won the war, even while we're still fighting battles like sin, conflict, or fear day to day.Sealed with a guaranteePaul says we have obtained an inheritance, and that the Holy Spirit is the guarantee, or down payment, of that inheritance until we fully receive it.Aaron compared it to a grandfather telling his grandchild that $50,000 has already been set aside for them, to be received at 25. The grandchild doesn't wonder if the money is coming. The promise and the paperwork are already real, even though the money isn't in hand yet. In the same way, we don't have to wonder if God's promises are coming. The Holy Spirit living in us is the proof.So who are we? We are people God chose before the world began. We are valued enough that God died for us. We don't have to fear the battle because the war is already won. And we are loved enough that God has given us a taste, through His Spirit, of what's still coming.Talk About It at HomeThese are the questions the group discussed. They work well for a longer conversation:What are some things people your age use to define who they are? Do you think those things can ever become too important? Why?Ephesians 1 tells us that we are chosen, loved, forgiven, and redeemed by God. Which of those truths is hardest for you to believe about yourself, and why?How could knowing that Christ has already won the war change the way you respond when you're dealing with fear, anxiety, temptation, or difficult circumstances?When the world tells you who you are, what can you do to remind yourself of what God says about you?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:If you had to describe yourself without mentioning your name, school, or activities, what would you say?What's one thing you've heard about God this week that stuck with you?Is there a promise from God that's hard for you to believe is actually true for you?What's one worry you're carrying right now that you could hand over to God?‍

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuSeptember 9, 2026The Gospel of JohnThe Crucifixion Part 2Aaron CapitoAbout the SeriesThis week continued the group's walk through the Gospel of John, landing on the final hours of Jesus' crucifixion.Passages: John 19:16-37What Was TaughtThe Walk to GolgothaJesus had already been beaten before He was ever nailed to the cross. His body was cut up and swollen, and He was made to carry the crossbeam itself, a piece of wood that likely weighed around a hundred pounds, for a long walk to the hill called Golgotha, the place of the skull, known to us in Latin as Calvary.He was crucified between two criminals, treated like the worst of society even though He had done nothing wrong.Pilate had a sign posted above Him that read, "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews." The religious leaders wanted it changed to say Jesus only claimed the title, but Pilate refused. The irony is that the "crime" they pinned on Jesus was true. He really was the King.His Mother, Cared ForWhile Jesus hung on the cross, soldiers gambled for His clothing, unknowingly fulfilling a prophecy written hundreds of years earlier that His garments would be divided by lot.Mary stood at the foot of the cross, watching her son die. In that moment, Jesus looked to her and to His disciple John and entrusted them to care for each other: "Woman, behold your son." "Behold your mother."Even in His suffering, Jesus was thinking about someone else. His love for His people was bigger than the pain He was in.It Is FinishedJesus said, "I thirst," and was given sour wine on a branch, fulfilling words written in the Psalms generations before. Then He said, "It is finished," and gave up His spirit.That phrase was not the cry of a man giving up. Think of finally reaching the end of a long story, like watching an entire movie saga and seeing every loose thread finally come together. "It is finished" was the moment everything God had promised, all the way back to the garden of Eden, reached its fulfillment.Not One Bone BrokenTo hasten death before the Sabbath, soldiers usually broke the legs of the men they crucified. When they reached Jesus, He was already dead, so His legs were left unbroken, exactly as an Old Testament prophecy said they would be. As the perfect Passover Lamb, Jesus had to be without blemish, and this detail confirmed it.A soldier pierced His side anyway, and blood and water came out, fulfilling yet another prophecy written centuries before.Jesus was not pretending, and He was not rescued at the last second. He gave every last drop He had. He gave Himself completely.Talk About It at HomeQuestions from group tonight:The disciples probably didn't think Good Friday was "good" while it was happening. Why do you think it's sometimes hard to see what God is doing when we're going through something difficult?Jesus was suffering on the cross, but He still made sure His mother was cared for. What does that tell us about Jesus' character? How can we reflect this in our own lives?Why do you think John keeps pointing out that things happening during Jesus' death fulfilled Old Testament Scripture? What does that teach us about God's plan?If you could remember only one thing from tonight's lesson the next time you're having a really difficult week, what would you want it to be?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:What's one part of the crucifixion story that stood out to you tonight?Why do you think it mattered that Jesus made sure His mom was taken care of, even while He was dying?Can you think of a time you kept caring about someone else even though you were having a hard day?What does "it is finished" mean to you?‍

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuJuly 1, 2026The Gospel of John The High Priestly Prayer Part 1Aaron CapitoAbout the SeriesStudents are continuing through the Gospel of John, working toward the story of the cross. This week, Aaron started a new section: John 17, the long prayer Jesus prayed with His disciples the night before His arrest. Since this prayer wasn't preached to a crowd but spoken privately to the Father, Aaron framed it as a rare chance to hear exactly what was on Jesus's mind hours before He died.Passages: John 17:1-12What Was TaughtJesus prayed for God's glory, not His own comfortAaron opened with a picture: imagine finding a letter your parents wrote about you that wasn't meant for you to read, or overhearing your coach talk about you when he didn't know you were listening. That's what it feels like to read John 17. We aren't hearing Jesus preach. We're overhearing Him pray.Jesus says "the hour has come," language John has been building toward through his whole Gospel, referring to the cross. Aaron pointed out that Jesus's first request wasn't to be spared from suffering. It was "glorify your Son, that the Son may glorify you." Jesus cared more about God's glory than His own comfort, which raised a challenge for students: when you pray, is your goal usually your own comfort, or God's glory?Jesus then defines eternal life in verse 3 as knowing God and Jesus Christ, not simply living forever or avoiding judgment. Aaron's point: eternal life isn't only something we receive when we die. It's a relationship with God that starts now. The real question for each student is whether they know about Jesus, or actually know Him.Jesus prayed specifically for His followersAaron explained that Jesus had manifested, or made clearly known, the Father's character to His disciples, and that they had received it and believed He was sent from God. Jesus then prays directly for them: that the Father would keep them, protect them, and make them one, even as He and the Father are one.Aaron noted that Jesus prayed this knowing exactly what His disciples would do in a few hours: panic, scatter, and in Peter's case, deny Him three times. Jesus wasn't praying for their physical safety alone. He was praying for their faithfulness, because nearly all of them would eventually be martyred for their faith anyway. And this wasn't a one-time prayer. Aaron pointed to Romans 8:34, where Paul says Christ is still interceding for us today. Jesus is still praying for His followers right now.Aaron closed by tying it to the Gospel itself: Jesus knew His disciples would fail Him and run, and He went to the cross anyway. Despite humanity's failure, God still sent His Son so we could be forgiven. Aaron encouraged students, with camp only a couple of days away, not to lose sight of that: even in His most stressful hours, Jesus still took time to pray for them.Talk About It at HomeThese are the questions the group discussed:If someone secretly listened to your prayers this week, what would they say is most important to you?Jesus said eternal life is knowing God. What's the difference between knowing about Jesus and actually knowing Him?How does it encourage you to know that Jesus still prays for His followers today?Jesus described His disciples as people who received His words and believed Him. What are some ways we can show that we really believe Jesus, not just say we do?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:If someone could hear everything you prayed about this week, what would surprise them?What's one way you can tell the difference between knowing facts about someone and actually knowing them?Does it feel different to think of prayer as a conversation instead of a list of requests?What are you most looking forward to, or nervous about, heading into camp?‍

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuAugust 17, 2025Redemption SeriesThe FloodLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight continued the Redemption Series into Genesis 6-9, following the line of Seth down to Noah, described as the one righteous man left on an increasingly corrupt earth. Tonight covered the flood that reset humanity and the covenant God made with Noah afterward.Passages: Genesis 6-9; Romans 1, 5; 2 Peter 3What Was TaughtA Grieved CreatorBy Genesis 6, human wickedness had spread so completely that Scripture says God was deeply grieved He had made mankind. This wasn't God losing control of His plan or being caught off guard, but it was still real grief over His creation's corruption. Sin, left unaddressed, spreads like a stain, and Romans 1 was used to show why judgment against that kind of unchecked sin becomes necessary.One Righteous ManNoah stood out as righteous, someone who walked closely with God in obedience, with three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Rather than wiping out humanity entirely, God chose to preserve a remnant through Noah's family, inviting him into His plan and establishing a covenant to save him, his wife, his sons, and his sons' wives through the coming flood.Building the ArkGod gave Noah detailed instructions to build a massive ark, roughly the size of the Titanic, with more than enough room for the animals it needed to carry. Noah's response was complete obedience, with no recorded complaining or resistance, a pattern that carried straight into the next chapter.Faith Before the RainIn Genesis 7, the animals came to Noah rather than Noah having to gather them himself, evidence of God's direct hand in the process. Once everyone and everything was inside, Noah and his family had to wait seven full days before the rain actually started, a real test of faith. All together, roughly a century passed between when God first told Noah what was coming and when the first rain finally fell.Forty Days and NightsThe flood began in Noah's six-hundredth year, with water bursting up from below and pouring down from above for forty days and nights, a number tied throughout Scripture to testing and purification. The same ark that meant salvation for Noah's family meant judgment for everyone else, and the text notes that God Himself shut the door, since only He determines who enters into salvation. As Noah entered the ark, the old corrupted world was being left behind for a renewed one, a picture of the same kind of renewal believers experience in Christ.A Flood Too Big to ImagineThe water eventually rose more than twenty feet above the highest mountains, wiping out every living thing outside the ark. The lesson pointed out that flood traditions show up in the stories of more than 200 cultures worldwide, most involving a catastrophic flood, a favored family, survival by boat, and animals being saved, treated as supporting evidence that the flood was a real, remembered event rather than only a myth confined to Genesis.Dry GroundThe water took about 150 days to fully recede, leaving the ark resting on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sent out a dove three times to check for dry land: first it found nothing and returned, then it came back with an olive leaf, and the third time it didn't return at all, signaling the earth was finally ready to be lived on again.A New BeginningGod told Noah's family to leave the ark and spread across the earth. The first thing Noah did once outside was build an altar and offer a costly sacrifice from the animals he'd just spent a year preserving, an act of real gratitude. Costly sacrifice matters to God not because He wants to take from His people, but because it reflects the same pattern of costly sacrifice Christ Himself would one day give. God promised never again to destroy all life with a flood, though the lesson noted one future judgment still remains, this time by fire at Christ's return rather than by water.The Rainbow and the CovenantIn Genesis 9, God renewed His original mandate to be fruitful and multiply, gave humanity authority over animals, permitted eating meat for the first time, and established that human life carries such weight, since people are made in God's image, that taking a life would carry the ultimate consequence. As the sign of this covenant, the third major covenant after the Edenic and Adamic, God placed a rainbow in the sky, a reminder of His promise of mercy both to us and, in a sense, to Himself. The lesson also noted that although the rainbow's meaning has been reshaped by today's culture, its original meaning as a sign of God's mercy hasn't changed, and encouraged staying grounded in that. The night closed by tying Noah's story to Romans 5: Noah's righteousness spared his family, and in the same way, Jesus' righteousness is what spares us. The flood cleaned the outside world. Only Jesus cleans us from the inside out.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.According to Romans 1, why is God's judgment necessary?What promise did God make to Noah after the flood, and what symbol did He give as a sign of this promise?How does Noah's obedience to God challenge the way you respond to God's instructions, especially when they don't make sense or seem difficult?The flood was God's way of wiping away the stain of sin. In what ways do you see God offering "new beginnings" in your own life? How should we honor God through those times?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Has waiting on something ever tested your patience with God?What does gratitude look like for you when things finally get better after a hard season?What's a "new beginning" you've had, and how did God show up in it?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuAugust 12, 2026The Gospel of JohnThe Betrayal and Arrest Part 2Aaron CapitoAbout the SeriesThis week's message continued in John 18, picking up right after Peter's first denial. It covers the high priest's questioning of Jesus, Peter's second and third denials, and Jesus' trial before Pilate.Passages: John 18:19-40What Was TaughtAn Unfair TrialThe message opened with a hypothetical: imagine being arrested for something you didn't do, giving a flawless defense that proves your innocence, but having a judge and jury who hate you decide you're guilty anyway. That's exactly what happened to Jesus. The perfect man, a perfect teacher, was condemned to death by people who hated Him despite having no real accusation against Him.Questioned by the High Priest (John 18:19-24)The high priest asked Jesus about His disciples and His teaching. Jesus said nothing about His disciples, protecting them, but spoke plainly about His teaching: He had always taught openly, in public, never in secret. When an officer struck Him for His answer, Jesus responded by challenging him to name the actual wrong in what He'd said.Jesus didn't just claim to be the Son of God. He backed it up, through Scripture, miracles, and eyewitnesses. His calm, composed response in the middle of an unjust arrest shows how much He loved the people putting Him through it.Peter's Second and Third Denials (John 18:25-27)Last week covered Peter's first denial. This week picks up with the second and third. The third one probably stung the most: the man who asked Peter about it was related to the servant whose ear Peter had cut off in the garden. The moment the rooster crowed, just as Jesus had predicted, Peter remembered, and Luke's Gospel adds that Jesus turned and looked at him. Peter went out and wept bitterly.It's easy to just feel bad for Peter here, but the point is bigger than that. Peter, one of Jesus' closest friends, hit rock bottom by denying Him to His face, and we do the same in smaller ways all the time: in sin, in staying quiet about our faith, and more. But Peter's denial isn't the end of his story. Even knowing it was coming, Jesus still went to the cross for Peter, and for us. Peter went on to become a bold, early leader in the church who eventually died for his faith. Our worst failure doesn't get the final word over Jesus' grace, for Peter or for us.No Accusation Against Him (John 18:28-32)There's an irony worth catching here: the religious leaders refused to enter Pilate's headquarters because it would make them ceremonially unclean for Passover, all while plotting to kill the God they claimed to serve. It's a good gut check for us too. Is our faith about looking religious, or about actually belonging to Christ? Character still matters, but it has to be powered by real faith, not the other way around.When Pilate asked what accusation they were bringing, he got nothing solid, and told them to judge Jesus by their own law instead. Jesus was headed for a criminal's death despite being innocent, and John points out this wasn't a surprise. It fulfilled what Jesus Himself had already said about how He would die. He wasn't a helpless victim. He was giving Himself up. What looks like total defeat to us was actually God accomplishing His greatest victory, even when it was hardest to see in the moment.My Kingdom Is Not of This World (John 18:33-40)Pilate asked Jesus directly if He was the King of the Jews. Jesus explained that His kingdom wasn't of this world: if it were, His followers would have fought to keep Him from being arrested. Instead, He came to testify to the truth, and He told Pilate plainly that He was born and came into the world for exactly this purpose.Pilate found no guilt in Jesus and offered to release Him as part of a Passover custom, but the crowd chose to free Barabbas instead, a man described as a robber and, more accurately in the original language, a terrorist. The crowd would rather free a violent criminal than the innocent man offering them salvation. That's how much the world hated Jesus for who He claimed to be, and Jesus told His followers to expect the same kind of hatred, since it hated Him first.The message's closing line: When you can't keep going, remember Christ did. Whatever hard thing we're walking through for following Jesus, He walked through something harder, and endured it for us.Talk About It at HomeUse these to keep the conversation going after service:What are some situations where Christians today might be tempted to hide the fact that they follow Jesus because they're afraid of what other people will think?The Jewish leaders cared about looking religious while rejecting Jesus. What does this teach us about the danger of caring more about looking like a Christian than actually following Christ?Our sticky point is, "When you can't keep going, remember Christ did." What is one situation in your life right now where you need to remember that?Peter failed Jesus in one of his lowest moments, but his failure wasn't the end of his story. Why is it important for us to remember that our failures don't have to be the end of our story with Jesus?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:What's something you were scared to admit was true, even though it was?Have you ever done the right thing even when it cost you something? What happened?Why do you think it matters more to actually follow Jesus than to just look like you do?What's one hard thing going on in your life right now where you need a reminder that God is still with you?‍

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuJuly 26, 2026Redemption SeriesThe WildernessLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight continued the Redemption Series, picking back up after the Golden Calf lesson from before camp. Where that lesson showed the consequence of one act of rebellion, tonight looked at what happens when rebellion becomes a pattern of life for Israel in the wilderness.Passages: Numbers 11, 13-14, 20-21; Psalm 95; John 3:14-15What Was TaughtCravings Over ContentmentA year after leaving Egypt, with the Law, the tabernacle, and a full year of God's provision behind them, Israel's first move in Numbers 11 was to complain, craving the food they used to eat in Egypt. God had been giving them manna every day, fresh and sufficient, but it wasn't enough for them.Students heard this compared to getting handed a brand new iPhone, fully paid for, and complaining because it wasn't the right color. God responded by providing quail, because He loved His people even in their complaining, but He also sent a plague on those who were craving. Many died and were buried in a place Israel named "the graves of craving." Their hearts weren't empty. They were just aimed at the wrong thing.Fear Over FaithIn Numbers 13, twelve spies scouted the Promised Land. Ten came back afraid, saying the people there were too strong to face. Two, Joshua and Caleb, came back with a different report, because instead of measuring the obstacle against themselves, they measured it against God. Israel sided with the fearful ten and talked about picking a new leader and going back to Egypt, despite having watched the Red Sea split and eaten bread from the sky every single day.God determined that generation would not enter the Promised Land. Instead, Israel would wander until it passed away, forty years as a direct consequence of a generation's unbelief. Rebellion here wasn't just breaking a rule. It was a functional distrust of God's character, treating the obstacle as bigger than God.Self-Reliance Over ObedienceIn Numbers 20, Israel was thirsty again, and God gave Moses a specific instruction: speak to the rock. Moses, frustrated, struck it twice instead and took credit for the miracle himself. For that, Moses, the most faithful man in Israel's history, the one who spoke with God face to face, was barred from ever entering the Promised Land.If Moses didn't get a pass in a moment of disobedience, no one earns their way into God's promises on their own. That is exactly why Israel, and we, need someone greater than Moses, someone who trusts and obeys God perfectly every time.From Judgment to HealingBy Numbers 21, Israel was complaining again, this time calling manna, the very thing keeping them alive, worthless. Students heard a personal example here: Liam shared that he prayed for his wife Caraline long before they met, prayed for her before their wedding, and still prays for her daily, yet still catches himself some days taking her for granted instead of staying grateful for the very thing he once prayed for.In response to Israel's complaint, God sent venomous snakes, and when the people cried out, He told Moses to lift a bronze serpent on a pole so that anyone who looked at it would live. Students heard this compared to antivenom, made from the very venom that's killing you, given in a controlled dose so the body can fight back and heal. Jesus points directly back to this moment in John 3:14-15: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that whoever believes in Him may have eternal life. The symbol of Israel's judgment became the means of their healing once it was lifted up. It was never about effort or fixing yourself first. It was look and live.Worship That Turns Into WarningThe night closed in Psalm 95, which opens with a call to worship God as Creator and Shepherd and then pivots into a warning that draws a straight line from Numbers to right now: "Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts."Four chapters, four rebellions, one pattern: God provides, and Israel doubts. Cravings over contentment. Fear over faith. Self-reliance over obedience, even from Moses. Complaints over gratitude. And every single time, God's response was both justice and mercy. He judged the sin, and He made a way through.Where This PointsStudents heard the true story of Maximilian Kolbe, a Catholic priest at Auschwitz in 1941. When the camp commander selected ten men to starve to death in retaliation for an escape, one of them, a husband and father named Francis Gajowniczek, broke down knowing he would never see his family again. Kolbe stepped forward and offered to die in his place. He spent his final days comforting the other men, and Francis survived the war, living until 1995 and spending the rest of his life telling people about the man who died for him.Kolbe volunteered once, for one man he didn't know. Jesus volunteered from before the foundation of the world, for people who were actively rebelling against Him, the whole book of Numbers included, and us. The question the group was left with: what are you doing with the fact that Jesus already did that for you? What do you want your default setting to be, complaint or confidence in Him?Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.Numbers 11 shows Israel craving something they already had good provision for. What's something good in your life right now that's stopped feeling like "enough" because you're craving something else?The ten spies let fear write their report instead of faith. Where is fear currently making one of God's promises feel smaller than your circumstances?Read John 3:14-15 next to Numbers 21. Why do you think Jesus specifically chose the bronze serpent to describe His own death, and what does "just look and live" mean for something you're currently trying to fix on your own?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:What's something good in your life that you've started taking for granted?Have you ever been so scared of a problem that it made you want to give up on something you'd already started?Who's someone you know who gave up something big for someone else? What was that like to watch?What does it look like for you personally to "look and live" instead of trying to fix something on your own?‍

chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuMay 31, 2026Redemption SeriesThe LawLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight continued the Redemption Series' move into the "Wilderness Transition," the stretch that covers Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy and closes out the Pentateuch. Tonight's focus stayed mostly in Deuteronomy, looking at Moses renewing the covenant with the next generation and what God's Law still means for us today.Passages: Deuteronomy 6, 28-30; Leviticus 19; Romans 7; Matthew 22What Was TaughtThe lesson opened with an illustration about a rule that felt like nothing but control, until a loss revealed it was actually love, meant to shape who you become. That's the shift for tonight: what if God's Law was never Him trying to control us, but Him showing us who we were always meant to be, and how much we need Him?The Law Was Always About Relationship, Not RulesMoses opens Deuteronomy 6 with the Shema: God is one, whole and complete, and His people are called to love Him with all their heart, soul, and strength. Above anything else, God wants our love. When His people truly love Him, everything else, time, effort, obedience, naturally follows. Leviticus 19 backs this up with two anchors: verse 2 calls Israel to be holy because God is holy, a relationship with Him, and verse 18 calls them to love their neighbor as themselves, a relationship with others. Jesus ties both together in Matthew 22 as the greatest commandments. The Law was never meant to be a checklist to finish. It's a heart posture meant to shape ordinary, everyday life.Blessings, Curses, and a Renewed CovenantIn Deuteronomy 28, Moses lays out real stakes: blessing for obedience, covering produce, livestock, land, and victory over enemies, and curses for disobedience. Israel would be so obviously blessed or cursed that the whole world would know only God could have caused it. God intended to reveal Himself to the world through His people. In Deuteronomy 29, He renews this covenant with the new generation, the children of those who died in the wilderness, making sure they knew He was still with them too.A Circumcised HeartIn Deuteronomy 30:6, Moses tells the people God will circumcise their hearts. Physical circumcision was an outward sign of an inward faith, similar to baptism, so a circumcised heart means God doing the deeper work of spiritual transformation Himself. We cannot be saved without God taking hold of our hearts, which is evidence that the Law was never meant to be the final word. It was a kickstarter for God's larger plan. Deuteronomy 30:19 makes clear the Law wasn't given to burden God's people, but to reveal who He is and expose our need for Him, so that we would choose Him.Free From the Law, Free for JesusTurning to Romans 7, Paul explains that before Christ, we were bound to obey the Law, but through His death, we became dead to the Law and free to live in Him. He compares it to marriage: a wife is bound to her husband until death, and only then is free to remarry without sin. In the same way, when Jesus, who perfectly fulfilled the Law, died, our relationship to the Law ended, and we became free to relate to Him as the risen Messiah instead.The Law as an X-RayPaul describes the Law as something like an X-ray: it exposes sin, but it isn't the cure, and you can't blame the X-ray for what it shows. We might never have recognized certain sin without the Law revealing it. The weakness was never in the Law, it's in us, and the enemy wants us to believe disobedience leads to a better life when it actually leads to death (Romans 7:12).Paul goes on in Romans 7:15-20 to name the real problem: it isn't a lack of desire, since we all want to do what's right, and it isn't a lack of knowledge either, since most of us know right from wrong. It's a lack of power. The Law can tell us what's good, but it can't give us the ability to do it. Paul's own cry in Romans 7:24 captures what happens to anyone trying to earn their way to God by being good: we try to use power we don't have, and it's impossible on our own. Verse 25 answers it: victory comes through Jesus. He doesn't remove the battle, but He carries us through it by His power.The Law is good. It shows us who God is, and it shows us who we are not. There's no receiving the healing of the gospel without first knowing you're sick. The Law still matters today, not as a checklist to complete, but as what reveals sin and points us toward a heart that loves God and loves others.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.Jesus summed up the whole Law as loving God and loving others. Which of those do you find most challenging right now, and why?The lesson contrasts obeying God as a checklist we work on until it's completed versus a heart posture. Where do you catch yourself slipping into checklist mode with God?When you're weighing a choice between the Lord's way or the world's way, what runs through your head? What things have authority over your decisions that aren't of the Spirit?Have you ever been discouraged or offended by what God's Word, like an X-ray, reveals in you? How should you respond instead?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Has a rule you didn't like ever turned out to be love in disguise?Do you tend to treat following God like a checklist, or does it feel more like a relationship?What's something about yourself that only became obvious once someone or something pointed it out?

chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuJune 10, 2026TopicalWhat The Bible Says About Heaven Aaron CapitoAbout the SeriesThis week's focus: what the Bible actually says about Heaven, versus what students may have picked up from movies, culture, or vague ideas about the afterlife.Aaron opened by asking students to think about the best ending they've ever seen in a movie, show, or video game, and why a satisfying ending matters so much to us. His example was Avengers: Endgame, where the hero's sacrifice resolves years of story at once. His point: we're wired to long for a good ending, and the Bible promises history has one, a real one, in Heaven.Passages: John 14:2-3, 6; Revelation 21:1-5, 21:23; Psalm 96:11-13; Philippians 3:20-21What Was TaughtHeaven is a real destinationAaron pointed to Jesus's words in John 14, where He says He is going to prepare a place for His followers in His Father's house. Aaron's challenge: Christians often spend far more time and energy thinking about relationships, phones, school, or what's next in life than they do thinking about what's actually coming. Heaven isn't a feeling or a concept. It's a real place we will consciously experience, without sin or its effects. Aaron compared it to the anticipation you feel the week before a vacation: if a temporary trip can make you that excited, how much more should an eternal one?Heaven is better than anything we knowAaron read from Revelation 21, where God promises to wipe away every tear, and death, mourning, crying, and pain will be gone for good. He pointed out how much of daily life is shaped by a broken world: sickness, broken relationships, anxiety, war. God promises to make all things new. Aaron compared it to a movie trailer: an amazing trailer still holds back the best parts for the actual film. Whatever we can imagine about Heaven, the real thing will be even better.The best thing about Heaven is GodAaron pushed back on the idea that Heaven is mainly about golden streets or mansions. The greatest reality of Heaven, according to Revelation 21:3, is that God will dwell with His people directly, forever, with nothing sinful straining that relationship. He compared it to visiting a celebrity's house: the house might be incredible, but you're really there for the person. In Heaven, we'll be amazed by the beauty of it all, but the real reason it's Heaven is that God Himself is there.Heaven gives us hope todayAaron closed with Philippians 3, where Paul reminds believers that their citizenship is in Heaven, even now. That reality is meant to change how Christians handle hard seasons. When life is difficult, we can remember that our suffering has meaning and won't last forever. When believers grieve the loss of a fellow Christian, they can grieve differently, knowing where that person now is.Aaron ended by addressing how someone actually gets to Heaven. Not by being a good person, going to church, or trying hard enough. He pointed to Jesus's own words in John 14:6, where Jesus says He is the way, the truth, and the life, and that no one comes to the Father except through Him. The hope of Heaven belongs to those who have placed their faith in Jesus, because of what His death and resurrection accomplished. Aaron's closing line to students: for the Christian, the best isn't behind us. It's ahead of us.Talk About It at HomeThese are the questions the group discussed:What is one thing from tonight's lesson that changed or challenged the way you think about Heaven?Why do you think God wants Christians to know about Heaven while we are still living on earth?If Heaven is our future home, how should that affect the way we live today?What is one area of your life where you need the hope of Heaven right now?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:What's the best movie or show ending you've ever seen, and what made it so good?What's one picture of Heaven you grew up believing that you're not sure is actually in the Bible?Is there something hard going on right now where it would help to remember it isn't forever?If you knew for certain Heaven was real, would it change anything about this week for you?‍

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuJune 7, 2026Redemption SeriesThe Law: Part 2Liam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight continued the Redemption Series' look at God's Law, picking up where last week left off: the Law was never meant to save us, only to reveal what holiness looks like and show that we can't reach it on our own. Tonight moved into the New Testament to see how Jesus fulfills that Law. Like a boundary meant to protect and guide, the Law was never the final destination. It was always pointing toward something greater, and that something is Jesus.Passages: Matthew 5-7; Mark 10; Luke 22What Was TaughtJesus Fulfills the Law, He Doesn't Cancel ItThe Sermon on the Mount opens with Jesus going up a mountain to teach, the same phrase used in the Greek Old Testament every time Moses went up Mount Sinai into God's presence. Moses went up to receive the Law and deliver it to the people. Jesus goes up as God Himself, delivering the deeper meaning behind it, fulfilling Moses' own words in Deuteronomy 18:15 that God would raise up a prophet like him.Just as the Law was never given to save Israel but to teach them how to live, the Sermon on the Mount isn't a plan for earning salvation. It's a picture of what life looks like under Jesus as King. In Matthew 5:17-20, Jesus says plainly that He came to fulfill the Law, not oppose it. The Greek word for fulfill means to bring something to its full, complete measure, exactly as it was always designed to be. Through Jesus, the Law moves from an external rulebook to something written on the heart.Performance vs. a Transformed HeartThe religious leaders of Jesus' day practiced legalism, strict obedience to the Law in an attempt to earn salvation through good works. It doesn't work, because none of us are obedient enough to get there on our own. Their righteousness was self-made, all external boxes checked, but Jesus said they were completely missing the point, because God has never been impressed by performance. He has always been after the heart. Legalism can make someone look right on the outside while leaving them empty within. Jesus isn't after a performance. He wants to transform a person from the inside so what comes out is real.Matthew 6:1 reinforces this: righteousness isn't for other people to notice, it's for the Father. What looks private and unnoticed to others is fully visible to God.The Golden Rule and the Narrow PathMatthew 7:12 gives the Golden Rule, treating others the way we'd want to be treated, and Jesus says this sums up the Law and the Prophets, tying back to loving God and loving others. Matthew 7:13-14 then contrasts two paths. The wide path is crowded with people trying to be good enough, doing enough right things to outweigh the wrong, and it feels responsible because everyone else is doing the same. Jesus says it leads to destruction anyway. The narrow path isn't narrow because it's complicated. It's narrow because it requires humbling yourself enough to admit you can't do it on your own.One way of putting it: imagine owing two million dollars you could never repay, and someone hands you a certified check covering every cent, no strings attached. The alternative is spending the rest of your life scraping together change, knowing you'll never make a dent. Trying to earn what God offers for free is choosing the second option. The chapter closes with the story of the wise and foolish builders (Matthew 7:24-27): obeying God builds a strong foundation, and ignoring Him leaves life unsteady.The Law Reveals, It Doesn't CureIn Mark 10, religious leaders tried to trap Jesus by asking about divorce. Jesus pointed them back to Moses but corrected how they were reading him, drawing out the difference between the letter of the Law, its exact wording, and the spirit of it, the deeper brokenness it was meant to address. Moses permitted divorce in cases of unfaithfulness because the Law had to account for human brokenness, but permitting something is not the same as commanding it.The Law works like a mirror, not a cure. It shows the problem, a hard heart, selfishness, a lack of love, without being able to fix it. Mark 10:27 points to the only one who can: only God can fulfill the Law's commands perfectly. The Law exposes what only grace can heal.The New CovenantLuke 22 moves into the New Covenant, made through Christ's own blood. His death was the final sacrifice required to pay for sin, fulfilling the Old Testament and the Law on our behalf. Communion was described as the public, ongoing reminder of that covenant.The lesson drew a direct line between the two Passovers. At the first, blood on the doorposts caused death to pass over Israel's homes, and a nation of former slaves was formed. At the cross, Christ's blood causes death to pass over everyone covered by it, and a people is formed from all who receive that payment, bound to God through His Son. The Law required blood because sin requires payment. The New Covenant goes further, offering an inner transformation that cleans us from sin and brings us close to the Father. Jesus meets every requirement the Law demanded: He is the standard, He took on our inability, and He became the sacrifice.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.Where in your life right now do you feel the biggest tension between what you want and what you know God's Word says?How does the cross change the way we read the Old Testament commands that feel heavy or impossible?Which ditch do you personally fall into more often: trying to earn God's favor by being "good enough," or using grace as a pass to take sin lightly? Explain.A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Do you feel like you have to earn love or approval, from God or from people? Where do you think that comes from?What's a rule in your life that actually protects you, even when it feels restrictive?Is it easier for you to look good on the outside or to actually feel right on the inside? Why?

chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuAugust 24, 2025Redemption SeriesThe TowerLiam HungateAbout the SeriesTonight closed out the last of Genesis' "Four Pillars," Creation, Fall, Flood, and now the Tower, picking up right after Noah's family left the ark and began to repopulate the earth.Passages: Genesis 10-11What Was TaughtNimrod, Hunter of MenGenesis 10 traces the families of Noah's three sons, and among Ham's descendants was Nimrod, whose name essentially means "let us rebel." Scripture calls him a powerful hunter before the Lord, but not as a compliment. The point made here was that Nimrod wasn't hunting animals, he was hunting people, using ruthless conquest to build a kingdom centered in Babylon, a place that would come to represent pride, oppression, and rebellion against God throughout the rest of Scripture and beyond.Come, Let Us BuildAt the start of Genesis 11, all of humanity still shared one language. As people migrated and settled in the land of Shinar, they decided to build a city and a massive tower, driven by one clear motivation in their own words: to make a name for themselves. That ambition directly defied what God had already commanded Noah's family after the flood, to be fruitful, multiply, and fill the earth, not cluster together and build a monument to themselves. It also reflected a lack of trust in God's promise never to flood the earth again. They even used the same waterproofing material Noah had used on the ark, on their own tower.God Steps InGod came down to see the city and tower being built, likely another appearance of the pre-incarnate Christ, taken seriously enough to address in person. He recognized that a unified humanity, if left unchecked, could accomplish anything it set its mind to, for better or worse, and history since has shown plenty of the worse: humanity's capacity for large-scale evil hasn't gone anywhere, from the Holocaust to 9/11 to global wars. So God confused their language and scattered them across the earth, stopping the project entirely.Judgment as MercyWhat can look like pure punishment here is really an act of mercy. By scattering humanity and slowing their collective rebellion, God protected people from where that unchecked ambition was heading, similar to a parent stepping in to stop a child from doing something that could seriously hurt them. Even in judgment, God's mercy was still at work, and that mercy is always evidence that His larger plan of redemption hasn't stopped moving.Every Nation, Tribe, and TongueGod didn't just scatter people, He confused their language too, which is where Babylon gets its name and where the word "babble" comes from. The lesson argued that human language is too complex, patterned, and specific to have simply been invented by people on their own, more evidence pointing to a divine origin rather than pure coincidence. As scattered groups settled into different environments over the generations that followed, distinct cultures and characteristics developed, the beginning of the kind of diversity we recognize today, framed here as a reflection of God's own creativity rather than an accident of history.A Setback, Not an EndThe bigger pattern across Genesis so far is hard to miss: the Fall, then Cain and Abel, then the flood, and now Babel, humanity repeatedly turning away from God even after being rescued by Him. Even so, God's response was never just to shut things down. One illustration used here: it's like being redirected mid-path, not to stop you completely, but to turn you around and point you the right way. The scattering at Babel wasn't the end of the story either. It set the stage for a future unity God would bring about, not through a tower built by human hands, but through Jesus, drawing people together from every nation, tribe, and tongue.Coming Up Next WeekThe story of a man who imperfectly but wholeheartedly pursued God's will.Talk About It at HomeThese are the same questions the group wrestled with tonight. They are a good way to keep the conversation going at the dinner table.Who was Nimrod, and what was the main motivation behind building the Tower of Babel?In what ways do you see pride and self-reliance influencing people's decisions today, just like they did for the people at Babel?Have you ever experienced a time when God redirected your path, even when it felt like a setback? How did it shape your faith?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:Have you ever wanted to "make a name for yourself" in a way that pulled you away from what actually mattered?What's a time a plan of yours got completely derailed, and it turned out to be for the best?What do you think it will actually look like when people from every nation and language are united in the end?

chunks.title: Landmark Church
chunks.text: Skip to main contentWatch LiveWatch LiveLiveDashboardDashboardDashboardenEnglish (United States)SpanishSearchMenuSeptember 16, 2026The Gospel of JohnThe Resurrection Part 1Aaron CapitoAbout the SeriesThis week students looked at the resurrection of Jesus, from His burial through His appearances to Mary Magdalene and the disciples. The story didn't end at the tomb, and the same hope the disciples found in the risen Jesus is available to us today.Passages: John 19:38-42; John 20:1-23What Was TaughtJesus Is BuriedJoseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus took Jesus' body, prepared it for burial, and laid it in a new tomb. John describes the scene with real finality. Jesus wasn't missing or in hiding. He was dead and buried.It's a lot like the funeral scene at the end of Avengers: Endgame. The whole world gathers to grieve someone who is truly gone. That's the weight John wants us to feel here. But unlike Tony Stark's story, Jesus' story wasn't over. Sometimes the darkest moment in a story comes right before its greatest moment.The Empty TombOn the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene found the stone rolled away and ran to tell Peter and John. Her first thought wasn't that Jesus had risen. It was that someone had stolen the body. Grave robbery was common in that world.Peter and John ran to the tomb and found it empty, with the burial cloths left behind and the face cloth folded neatly by itself. Robbers don't unwrap a body and fold the cloth before they leave. Something else happened here.The cross reminds us Jesus died for us. The empty tomb reminds us He defeated death for us.Mary Meets the Risen JesusMary stayed at the tomb weeping. She saw two angels, then turned and saw Jesus himself, but didn't recognize Him until He said her name. That wasn't unusual. Jesus often wasn't immediately recognizable after He rose. The disciples on the road to Emmaus, and later at the lake of Tiberias, didn't know Him right away either.Jesus told Mary not to cling to Him but to go tell the disciples He was ascending to "my Father and your Father, my God and your God." Because of what Jesus accomplished, those who trust Him get the same access to God the Father that Jesus has.Mary went from mourner to messenger. She told the disciples, "I have seen the Lord." Jesus turns our tears into a testimony.Jesus Appears to the DisciplesThe disciples were hiding behind locked doors, afraid for their lives. Jesus came and stood among them, showed them His nail-pierced hands and His wounded side, and said, "Peace be with you." Then He breathed on them and gave them the Holy Spirit, sending them out the same way the Father had sent Him.Notice the order: Jesus comes to them. Jesus gives them peace. Jesus shows them He's alive. Then Jesus sends them. The resurrection didn't erase their fear. It gave them something bigger than their fear: Jesus Himself.My own father was a believer who passed away in the summer of 2022. That loss brought real grief. But because Jesus is risen, I don't have to believe death was the end for my dad. His faith in Christ means death didn't get the final word. That's the same hope Jesus gave the disciples in that locked room, and it's the hope He gives us. Whatever we're facing, fear, grief, uncertainty, even death itself, Jesus holds it. Because He's alive, we can face tomorrow with hope.Talk About It at HomeThese are the questions students discussed tonight.What would you have thought if you were one of the disciples and saw the empty tomb?Why do you think Jesus wanted Mary and the disciples to tell others that He was alive?Mary went from being afraid and sad to telling everyone about Jesus. How can we share our hope in Jesus with others?How does knowing that Jesus rose from the dead give you hope when you are afraid, sad, or going through something difficult?A few easier openers if you want to start smaller:What's your favorite part of the Easter story?Has anyone ever told you good news that was almost too good to believe?If you could ask Jesus one question about the resurrection, what would it be?When has hope helped you get through something hard?‍
